Canadians who would like to show their displeasure with the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal.
The petitioners say; whereas the Mulroney Government has sold out Canada and received nothing in return; whereas Canadian industries are still not protected from U.S. trade laws; whereas the United States obtained everything it wanted in all key sectors, especially agriculture, energy, auto trade, financial services and investment; and whereas thousands of Canadian jobs are threatened and the Conservative Government has not provided for any adjustment assistance for Canadian workers, the undersigned, your petitioners, humbly pray and call upon Parliament to denounce the Government for signing the Mulroney-Reagan trade agreement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by a large number of residents of Ontario and Saskatchewan with respect to the fact that the Conservative Government had no mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a free trade agreement with the United States. They note that this agreement would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future and undermine our ability to build a society distinct from that of the United States.
They therefore call upon Parliament to dissolve and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed free trade agreement during a national general election.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have a second group of petitions signed by many hundreds of concerned Canadians from across this land who note that the Canadian Government funded unethical brainwashing experiments by the late psychiatrist, D. Ewen Cameron, which were conducted at Allan Memorial Institute in Montreal in the 1950s and early 1960s.
They note that many Canadians were permanently damaged by these experiments that were inflicted upon them without their knowledge or consent, and that the Canadian Government has refused to accept any legal or moral responsibility to these Canadians, or offer any reparation.

January 21, 1988
Petitions
They call upon Parliament to immediately release to the Canadians all the incriminating evidence it has to assist them in their lawsuit, to offer financial assistance and to publicly acknowledge its legal and moral responsibilities to these Canadians.
This is particularly significant in light of the important victory these people had in the federal district court in the United States just a couple of days ago, which I am sure all Canadians celebrate.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is my pleasure and indeed honour to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 106 from a number of constituents who are concerned that the Conservative Government does not have a mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a trade deal with the United States.
They believe that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised, in the course of negotiations that Canada would retain its sovereignty. They feel that it has now been compromised severely.
They also believe that the trade deal would deny Canada the policy freedom to determine its own economic future, and thereby undermine Canada's ability to build a society distinct from that of the United States.
They also believe that it denies Canada the secure access to the American market which in fact was the key objective in the negotiations.
Since it also threatens the loss of hundreds of thousands of jobs, these petitioners are calling upon Parliament to dissolve now to allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed trade deal in a national general election.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday, when the House interrupted its proceedings, I was talking about the need for improving the road system in the Maritimes or, I should say, the Atlantic provinces.

There is a need. It has been shown that the road system in the Atlantic area is deteriorating at a very alarming rate. That is because it was not made to support the kind of traffic which is being transported over that surface. Of course, it would be one of the objectives of the agency to look at the infrastructure of the transportation system.
The Savoie Report made the recommendation that the agency look at transportation policies and promote efficient modes of transportation. As you know, Madam Speaker, our transportation system is one of the prime components of a sound regional development program. The agency will not be able to undertake with its own moneys-the $1.05 billion over five years-the type of work that would have to be done. However, it could recommend to the Government that this work be done under IRDA agreements. I hope that the agency will look into this matter.

In concluding, Madam Speaker, I am confident that if the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is given a certain autonomy by the Government, the kind of autonomy recommended by the Savoie Report, the agency will undoubtedly have a positive impact on economic development in Atlantic Canada. However, if the agency were to become just another level of government bureaucracy, and the Savoie Report warns us of this danger, I believe it would lose much of its effectiveness and a great deal of its credibility.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam. Speaker, I wonder if the Hon. Member would care to comment on the attitude that seems to have been expressed by the Government toward the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and, indeed, toward the problems of Atlantic Canada. The Minister responsible for ACOA, who is a Senator, seems to have agreed with another Minister, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes), that this agency and the $200 million per year being poured into it is the last kick at the can for Atlantic Canada. It seems that in having this attitude toward Atlantic Canada the Government has taken it off the national priority list, which is where it should be.
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
The Government fails to recognize that the Economic Council of Canada has said that the most serious economic problem for the country in the coming years will be that of uneven regional development. Will the Hon. Member comment on that aspect of this matter? The comments of the Minister responsible for the agency, who agreed with and, in fact, quoted the Minister of Public Works, do not seem to indicate a serious attitude-that we will put in money and wait for four or five years, as the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) said, and see if it will work. The amount of money committed to this agency seems to indicate an attitude on the part of the Government that it does not take this matter seriously at all.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to thank the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. Harris) for his question. I share his concerns, and I think it is too bad a Minister should have made these comments because the Atlantic region has been living with the problem of regional disparity for a long time. We have a long history of trying to reduce the disparity between the Atlantic region and the central, more developed part of Canada. We have tried a number of solutions. In some cases we have been successful, in others perhaps not as successful.
To say that the Agency is our last chance and to put this as a kind of ultimatum to the people of Atlantic Canada, meaning: We are going to give you the money, we are going to give you a number of resources, including this agency, and if you don't make it this time, that's it. I find it very difficult to accept this attitude on the part of the Government.
Madam Speaker, I sincerely hope the agency will find ways to help the people of Atlantic Canada, not as a last resort but as an agency that for a certain period of time will support efforts to enhance regional and economic development in the Atlantic region.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerald S. Merrithew (Minister of State (Forestry and Mines)):
subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am delighted to take part in the debate on second reading of Bill C-103, an Act to increase opportunity for economic development in Atlantic Canada, to establish the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation and to make consequential and related amendments to other Acts. I am delighted for several reasons. Number one, this is one of the first pieces of legislation in our new year, 1988. We think in Atlantic Canada, and we think as a Government of Canada, that this is an immensely important piece of legislation, and one which will undoubtedly have major benefits for the people of Atlantic Canada.
In introducing my comments, perhaps as many other people in the House, I have had some considerable experience politically in my 17 years in public life. I have had the pleasure, the opportunity, and the privilege to serve municipally for 12 years in the provincial Government of New Brunswick, with a good deal of that time as a Minister, and of course to serve in the Government of Canada. It is a rare privilege indeed.
Throughout that particular time I have followed with a great deal of interest developments in terms of the governments at all levels attempting to deal with the issue of regional disparities and the inequality of opportunities we have in Canada. I have lived with that. As a Minister, I was responsible for economic development in the province for some six years, so I have had to deal with a good number of different governments and different Ministers, and a good number of
different measures and initiatives by governments to try to redress those anomalies.
I have lived through and watched as successive governments have indicated and introduced all sorts of agencies, programs, initiatives, and Acts to redress regional disparities. I remember very well the Atlantic Development Board. It did certain things for our region. 1 remember the ARDAs, the Agriculture Rural Development Agreements in the 1960s. 1 remember very well in politics when DREE was established. That was supposed to be the panacea for addressing regional development. That was to be the one government Department that was solely responsible for addressing regional disparities.
I was the Minister of Commerce and Development in the province when in 1981 then Prime Minister Trudeau announced, with some fanfare, that we no longer had a need for DREE and that every government department was now going to be responsible for regional development. They were themselves going to monitor and assist in dealing with regional development issues in those provinces and regions of Canada where disparities existed.
At that time I did not make a political condemnation of that particular statement. I said that I would wait. Ironically, I would have to say in retrospect, and historically, that what we expected at the time, to have every government department interested in regional development, simply did not happen to the extent that it should.
I have signed many GDAs, general development agreements, in history. I have signed many of the sub-agreements under the ERDA process. I have had the pleasure of doing that both as a provincial Minister and as a federal Minister. I can remember very well the RDIA, the Regional Development Incentives Act when it was introduced, and subsequently a program under that Act, 1RDP. I have worked with it. I have worked with companies, institutions, and organizations that have applied for assistance under that particular Act.
Over the years I have seen many initiatives tried that to some extent have worked. I know that there are some people in Canada who say that nothing will work in Atlantic Canada. Having been close to it, I absolutely disagree with that. To a certain degree every one of those particular initiatives has worked. In some way or another they have all closed the gap in terms of opportunities and earned incomes in my region of Canada. To some extent we can take credit in governments for having achieved some measure of success, and I will deal with that later.
I was most delighted when on October 1, 1986 our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) put in the Throne Speech a statement which I understand he drafted himself. It shows the type of interest and commitment that our Prime Minister has taken in regional development when he put in the Throne Speech the following comment:
January 21, 1988

It is time to consider new approaches, to examine how our considerable and
growing support for Canada's regions can be used more efficiently, more
effectively and with greater sensitivity to local conditions and opportunities.
Out of that this piece of legislation grew. What we are dealing with today in the establishment of ACOA or the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is, in my view, most welcome. It is a new and daring change from previous initiatives, and I think it will work.
This legislation we are dealing with today gives certain powers over the 1RDP, which is still in effect; it gives powers over the Atlantic Enterprise Program. I happened to be there when one of the previous Ministers of DRIE made that announcement publicly in Moncton, New Brunswick. I supported it and helped draft and make changes to it, and 1 think it is an excellent program. It will undertake the Enterprise Cape Breton Program, and of course the ERDAs and successive agreements to the ERDAs. The program that has been passed over to this particular agency is challenging. It will be useful, and in the long run I think it will be very workable and useful for Atlantic Canada.
This legislation is based on six major principles, the first being the principle of consultation. We have done that more than any Government in the history of this country. We have done it through the efforts of Dr. Donald Savoie, of the University of Moncton. We have done it with municipalities, with the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council, with the Atlantic Provinces Chamber of Commerce, with the Conseil Economique du Nouveau Brunswick, with the Economic Development Council of Newfoundland, with boards of trade, chambers of commerce, municipalities, provincial Governments, and the Council of Maritime Premiers. Nobody but nobody can deny that this legislation and this particular agency was born and is the fruit of considerable consultation.
The second principle is that, for a change, we wanted to make sure the decision-making would come from the region itself. I am delighted that 90 per cent of the decisions that will be made and have been made to date will be made in the region. Those decisions are considerable. There have been 451 approvals to date with tens of millions of dollars going to regional development.
The third principle is that we will direct our efforts to a field which I think is very apropos, and that is towards small and medium sized businesses. That is the basis and the ground work for development in our region. In my own home province 90 per cent of all of the enterprises are owned and developed by New Brunswickers. We think that is an important initiative and that there is a great deal of potential for future growth in the small and medium sized businesses of Atlantic Canada.
The fourth principle is that regional programs are adapted to regional needs. That is very important. We do not need Ottawa, we do not need the mandarinate, we don't need anyone to tell us what we need in Canada. We have had that for years and years and years. The business people of Atlantic Canada are the ones who know best how to deal with the issues
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
of Atlantic Canada and how to make things work in Atlantic Canada. It is not quite the same as other parts of Canada. We have our own unique situations that need to be dealt with on a regional basis. Therefore, the programs will be adapted to regional needs in our region.
Another basic principle is one of creating an environment for business to flourish on its own. Over and over again I have said to the Board of Trade in the City of Saint John, New Brunswick, my home city, a city which I have represented politically for some 17 years, that it cannot expect government to do everything for it. We cannot expect governments to redress all anomalies in terms of equality in Canada. We cannot expect governments to do everything for us. However, what we can do is create the environment for our private sector to do what is necessary to create jobs and to create prosperity in our region.
We have done that. We have put in place policies, all sorts of new programs, and the kind of climate which is conducive to Atlantic businesses to invest, to create jobs, to create new enterprises, to make money, and to create investment and profit in the region.
The sixth principle would be flexibility. We want this piece of legislation. I do not think there has been another one like it in the history of Canada dealing with regional development and allowing more flexibility. I am pleased to serve with Senator Lowell Murray, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie), and my other five colleagues in the federal Cabinet from the region, on a board which discusses the initiatives, policies, and programs we think are needed for regional development.
I suppose the seventh principle is not spelled out specifically. We want the particular agency, as we want the board which serves the agency, to have a co-ordinating role and function in regional development. I do not believe that this agency is the sole agency responsible for regional development. 1 expect every department in the Government of Canada to be aware of and to be concerned with regional development. I am pleased to say that largely they are concerned. We have had exceptional co-operation from Ministers and departments in the Government of Canada.
Perhaps the seeds of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency might have sprung from a conference, a convention, a meeting, or an initiative which we undertook in September 1986 called "The Atlantic Focus". At that time the Atlantic government caucus, the Progressive Conservative caucus, met with the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council. We also met with the Chambers of Commerce of the Atlantic Provinces, the Council of Maritime Premiers, the Governments of the four provinces, the Conseil Economique du Nouveau Brunswick, and the Economic Development Council of Newfoundland, and we listened. I take some pleasure in saying that as a result of "The Atlantic Focus" initiative which we undertook at that

January 21, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
time, the Prime Minister listened and agreed-and I agree- that we must have new directions and new initiatives in this region.
We have undertaken all sorts of new programs. The previous speaker mentioned the expenditure of some $200 million per year. That figure is not correct. The correct figure is about $400 million per year. We have said that the $1.05 billion was additional new dollars. That was repeated over and over again by the Prime Minister and by other government Ministers. It will be over and above the expenditures we have, which will be around $200 million per year under the IRDA process and others.
Our Government supports equality through all sorts of programs such as our equalization program, our Established Programs Financing, and other initiatives taken by line departments in the Government. The dollars allocated to regional development are significantly more than ever before. I am pleased to say that we think the dollars are reasonably adequate. It is a refreshing increase in what the previous Government provided for regional development. It will go a long way toward meeting the needs of Atlantic Canadians.
The board which has been set up by the Ministers responsible in governrrtent has 1$ members, all of whom are established, successful business people and public servants in the region. They are dealing very effectively with the policy, programs, and philosophy-what we are trying to do with ACOA. I can tell the House that we acted very swiftly in that regard. The Prime Minister announced the ACOA initiative in late June, 1987. By August 31, 1987 we had named the board, and three days later that board was meeting in Moncton, New Brunswick dealing with the problems faced in Atlantic Canada. It is still dealing with them. In fact, it has had four meetings, and I will be attending a meeting with them on Monday and Tuesday of next week in Halifax.
There are many things I could say, because I am truly very interested in regional development. However, I want to conclude my remarks by indicating why I am so supportive of this piece of legislation. I support Bill C-103 because it gives a formal, legal status to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. It is needed. I support Bill C-103 because it outlines the very considerable, new, and flexible powers of the agency, far surpassing the power of any previous regional development mechanism or agency. I have worked with them and I have studied a good deal about them. It represents the very real and strong commitment of the Prime Minister and the Government to combating disparities in our region and to fostering economic prosperity in Atlantic Canada.
I support it because it was conceived, nourished, and developed in the Atlantic region to serve and assist our businessmen, our entrepreneurs, and indeed all Atlantic Canadians. It grew out of a wide consultative process with those who know our region, with those who live in our region, with those who invest in our region, with those who work in our region, and with those, above all, who understand our
region and the difficulties, problems, and challenges we face there.
The form in which the legislation is before the House is a direct consequence of the consensus we reached together after consultation. It was not foisted on Atlantic Canada by Ottawa. It was developed in the region by Atlantic Canadians and by our citizenry. Atlantic Canadians wanted the right to plan their own destiny, not to have it dictated to them. It reflects the commitment of the Prime Minister to a new approach in regional development and to economic growth in Atlantic Canada as he outlined in the Speech from the Throne. It is an affirmation of our Government's commitment to developing the most important resource in Atlantic Canada-our people.
Bill C-103 will challenge Atlantic Canadians to show all Canadians their initiative, their enterprise, and their willingness to work hard to improve their lot in this wonderful country in which we live and to share in the wealth and prosperity which we know is not being equally shared today.
In closing I want to quote from an editorial which appeared in a Saint John newspaper, one of my own newspapers. It reads: "The ball has been placed squarely in Atlantic Canada's court". I have no doubt whatsoever as an Atlantic Canadian that Atlantic Canada will rise to meet that challenge.

speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, it is interesting that the recent speaker for the Government was the Hon. Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew). In that title is a part of the problem about which we are talking today.
During the election campaign of 1984 the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised the people of Canada that when he formed the Government he would create a full ministry of forestry. He indicated that forestry was an important industry for the entire country and particularly for the regions of the country. Today, nearly four years later, there is no full ministry of forestry. There is no full minister of forestry. With all due respect to my colleague, who is a very nice person, the fact is that he is the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines.
We are talking about the two major enterprises found in the regions of Canada, mining and forestry. The Government does not even have a full ministry of mines, let alone a full ministry of forestry. Therein lies the real concern of this Government for regional economic development in Canada.
If the Government were serious, it would have lived up to the promise it made to the people of Canada, and particularly those of us from the regions of Canada, to form a full ministry of forestry. That has not occurred. Today, forestry is handled by a Ministry of State. This means that a handful of people work with the Minister on forestry and a handful of people work with the same Minister on mines. Of course, the Department is relegated far down in the hierarchy of cabinet power. Forestry and mining are at the bottom of the pile.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Forestry, the largest industry in Canada.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
As my hon. friend from Skeena so aptly reminds Hon. Members, the largest export industry in Canada in terms of value is the forestry industry. It is one of the major employers in the country, employing hundreds of thousands of Canadians directly and hundreds of thousands of Canadians
indirectly in every single region. Yet the Prime Minister does not feel that this is an important enough industry to have a full Minister. Therein lies the problem that we are debating in the House of Commons today.
Bill C-103 is an Act to establish the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. That is really the wrong heading for this agency. It should actually be something like "The Atlantic Canada Smoke and Mirrors Agency", or the "The Atlantic Canada Hoax Agency".
This Bill in no way advances the cause of removing economic and regional disparities in Canada. As a matter of fact, I will attempt to make the case, as my hon. colleagues have before me, that this initiative by the Government will actually widen the gap in economic activity between Atlantic Canada and central Canada. That is exactly what has happened over the last little while.
I just finished reading a report written by Elizabeth Beale, the chief economist of the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council. She has recently reported that there has been very little improvement in any of the major indicators of regional disparity between the Atlantic provinces and the country as a whole since the 1960s, She goes on to make the point that the gap in the unemployment rate is proportionately the same as it was 15 years ago.
In a very objective, honest, fair, factual presentation, the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council has said that the situation faced by residents of Atlantic Canada has not changed since the 1960s and that the regional and employment differences are no different than they were 15 years ago. That is a real condemnation, not only of the actions of this Government but of the actions of the previous federal Governments since the 1960s when these statistics were first collected.
At one time or other most Canadians have read Hugh MacLennan's book, Two Solitudes, which makes the case for the French and the English realities of Canada. It seems in so many ways that there is now a new kind of two solitudes, a new two-tier Canada composed of southern Ontario and the rest of Canada, southern Ontario and the hinterland, southern Ontario, which is the industrial heartland, and the resource-based regions of Canada. That is the reality.
Not long ago The Globe and Mail said that despite the federal Government's assurances that economic renewal is working for all Canadians, more than 95 per cent of the additional jobs created last year were located in one province, the Province of Ontario. It is incredible that 95 per cent of all new jobs created in Canada were created in the Province of Ontario, and to be more specific, in the greater Toronto area. We do recognize that the large Province of Ontario has incredible regional variations in economic development and growth as well, particularly between the metropolitan area of Toronto and the rest of the province, particularly northern Ontario.
January 21, 1988

In the same article it was indicated that last week the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) acknowledged that the benefits of Conservative economics have not been evenly shared across the country. The Minister of Finance has agreed that everything is okay in his constituency and in downtown Toronto where the unemployment rates today are virtually nil, but for the rest of the country things are not going terribly well. Therein lies the essence of the problem.
As the gap between unemployment levels in central Canada and unemployment levels in the rest of Canada increases, we see the emerging challenge that will face Canadians in the decade to come. The Economic Council of Canada in its recent report pointed out that the major economic problem facing Canada is the tremendous difference in economic prosperity between central Canada and the rest of the country. This is the challenge that we must face.
I suppose that this is the challenge the Government has attempted to take on by creating this Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. Let us put this into context. As the Hon. Minister of State for Forestry and Mines indicated, the Government plans to provide $200 million per year to Atlantic Canada to assist it in its economic development, and $200 million per year might sound like a great deal of money to many people, and of course it would be a lot of money to many people. Let us put that into context because $200 million per year over five years comes to $1 billion. However, in every year of the last three years the federal Government has taken $1 billion of existing programs out of Atlantic Canada. Three years ago it took out $1 billion, last year it took out $1 billion and this year it took out $1 billion. Now it is saying it has some great news, it will give Atlantic Canadians $200 million and they are supposed to be thankful because this is supposed to be helpful. That is the reality. This is the hypocrisy with which we are dealing.
I think the Prime Minister should come clean and tell the people of Atlantic Canada that the Government has taken away many of the programs that existed in the past to assist economic development, but it will give back a pittance and is asking the people to be thankful for that.

Who is the Minister responsible for this new agency? speechtext:
He is not in jail or anything like that, he is in the other place. I cannot use the name of the other place, but we know what that is, the other part of Parliament. That means that this critical Minister responsible for economic development in Atlantic Canada will not be subject to questions from members of the Government or the Opposition in the House of Commons. He will not have to stand here and explain why the funding going into this agency is so low. He is hidden away, closeted away, if you like, in the other place, far from any scrutiny, well apart from the people he is attempting to assist.
That is not right in a democracy. In a democracy people expect that Ministers responsible be in their places so that they can be held accountable for their actions. That is the way democracy works.
I suggest that when you are not sure that what you have done is correct, when you are trying to pull a smoke and mirrors trick on the people of a certain region, when you are perpetuating a hoax on the people of a region, you do not want to have a cabinet Minister in the House of Commons. You want that Minister to be in the other place where he can hide away from criticism, scrutiny, and evaluation. That is what Senator Lowell Murray said he was going to do. He said that he was going to be in charge of this operation and that the decisions would be made by him. That is, of course, a very undemocratic approach to this whole matter.
In his opening speech the Minister of Transport indicated that the majority of these funds would go to small and medium businesses in Atlantic Canada. Members on all sides of the House would endorse grants or special loans being given to small and medium businesses. I listened with interest to my friend, the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines, who laid out a long list of initiatives of which he had been a part in his

January 21, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
previous life as a provincial Minister and as a Minister in the Government today. He listed all the infrastructure which the Government was providing and how important that is.
That is one of the shortcomings in the terms of reference of this agency. There is no quarrel that a good deal of funding and support ought to go to assist small and medium businesses, to develop new products, and to conduct market research with regard to new market opportunities, but we must also develop critical infrastructure in this day and age.
1 read a report the other day of a survey of a number of young Canadians. When they were asked in Atlantic Canada what the most important natural resource of Atlantic Canada was the overwhelming response was cod fish or fishing. That same question was put to people on the Prairies who said that grain was the most important natural resource. In British Columbia some people said it was trees and forests.
The most important natural resource of Atlantic Canada and all of Canada are the people, particularly the young people. I believe that a lot of this support ought to be going to develop that natural resource, for the infrastructure for education, skill development and sophisticated training to develop research and development. That is the kind of infrastructure that the economy of the future will require as we move toward a knowledge-based economy and the year 2000. However, this agency does not have a major mandate to provide that necessary skill development and R and D infrastructure.
Another thing that is absent is a real commitment to lower the rates of unemployment in Atlantic Canada. We assume that in a few months from now we will be having a general election. A New Democratic Party government would set targets in Atlantic Canada. A New Democratic Party government with Ed Broadbent as Prime Minister would recognize that decade after decade programs have obviously not reduced the economic and regional differences between Atlantic Canada and regional Canada and that the levels of unemployment continue to be excessively high, decade after decade, because governments have not been serious in their efforts to reduce unemployment and produce economic prosperity for Atlantic Canada. A New Democratic government would set targets. It would commit itself to reducing the levels of unemployment in Atlantic Canada by a certain percentage point within the first year, the second year, and the third year until the unemployment levels in Atlantic Canada were zero. That would be our stated goal. We would set out a very specific annual strategy to achieve that goal. Each year we would ask whether we had been successful. We would be accountable as to whether we were successful in reducing the levels of unemployment. If we were not, we would increase our efforts toward those goals about which we would be serious.
However, the Government does not set any goal. If we were to evaluate this program five or ten years from now and found that the levels of unemployment had been reduced by half a percentage point or had perhaps even increased, there would
be no way of determining whether the initiatives were adequate and successful. If you have no goal, no objective, how do you know whether you have been successful?
This is like starting off on a vacation, just getting into a car and driving off without any idea of where you are going, just aimlessly driving down the road. That is what this Atlantic agency is really all about. It is a rudderless ship moving about the harbour. It is a person driving along without any particular destination in mind.
It is critical that targets be set in order that unemployment levels in Atlantic Canada be reduced annually by a specified amount. We should set such goals, not only for Atlantic Canada but for the nation as a whole, for all the regions that are having difficult times.
One of the critical points which the Minister of State failed to mention in his comments involves government procurement. One of the tools which a government has, to give encouragement and support, to show that it cares, is government procurement targeted at all levels, local businesses and industry. In that way markets can be provided which will really assist new businesses and industries in particular.
In the trade deal with the United States we signed away the right to target government procurement programs to Atlantic Canada as we should. In other words, everything that all levels of government need in Atlantic Canada should be procured from that area. Whether they are goods or services, as long as they are reasonably competitive, the businesses and industries of that area should be given an advantage. We signed away that right. We have said that any company in the United States will be able to bid on government procurement programs. We have now signed away in the trade deal the one obvious vehicle that governments have to assist local business.
In closing, much more can be done. Many more steps can be taken to assist the development of Atlantic Canada. Let me quote what John Crow, Governor of the Bank of Canada, said recently: "Many of these regional imbalances that presently exist could eventually drag down the whole economy of the country". In other words, if we do not seriously address these regional differences in terms of economic development and growth, it could drag down the entire Canadian economy. That is our primary challenge.
1 am afraid that this initiative by the Government in Bill C-103, to establish the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, falls far short of meeting that goal of reduced economic inequalities that exist in Canada.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, let me congratulate the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) on his speech. He and all Members in this Party are concerned about regional development, as I am sure are all Members. However, the Government's measures do not seem to match the size of the problem.
January 21, 1988

Will he comment on another aspect of regional development that could assist the regions of Canada, particularly the Atlantic region in this case, and that is the allocation of the Public Service in this country? Thirty per cent of the federal Public Service in Canada is located in Ottawa, which is very highly centralized compared to other countries such as the United States where only 12 per cent of the public service is located in Washington.
There have been some decentralization experiments in Canada in the past, but these have been halted. The results of those studies have found that these units operating outside of Ottawa have been more efficient in terms of the complement of person-years required to do the job, the stability of the workers, and the lack of turnover compared to the experience in Ottawa. They seem to be successful not only in improving the efficiency of the Public Service of Canada but in spreading some of the funds and jobs of the federal Government throughout the country, particularly to areas where employment in the private sector and other sectors of the economy is difficult to obtain.
Would the Hon. Member comment on that method of contributing to reducing regional disparity in this country?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member has posed a very interesting question. Let me reflect for a moment on part of the problem we face in this country in dealing with economic discrepancies in terms of growth. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) comes from Toronto and has surrounded himself with some very well intentioned, serious bureaucrats. But I do no believe the Minister actually understands what it is like in the regions of Canada. Considering the constituency of the Minister of State for Mines and Forestry, I suspect that he would have a better understanding.

They are not temporary jobs; while the problem facing individuals who do not have a job is severe, it is not alleviated with six months of useless work. subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to participate in the debate on Bill C-103. I view this legislation as marking a crossroads in the economic evolution of Atlantic Canada within our Confederation. There are many people in this House from Atlantic Canada who sit here because they have a mandate from their constituents to work for and to achieve improved economic opportunities for their constituents. I am no exception.
I became interested in politics because I took the view as a young Atlantic Canadian that things could be better, that there were new ways which could be tried and that success and progress was an attainable goal. I did not accept that we as Atlantic Canadians were destined always to be the have-not region within Confederation. I took that message to my constituents in 1984 and they agreed.
Today we are debating a piece of legislation that reflects a very carefully taken policy decision by our Government that this is a better way to go. Let us look at precisely what Bill C-103 prescribes and what principles it outlines by way of a regional development strategy. First, let us look at the goals. There are some speakers who have said this legislation does not prescribe a goal, but the goal is outlined in Clause 4 which states:
The purpose of this Part is to increase opportunity for economic development in Atlantic Canada and, more particularly, to enhance the growth of
earned incomes and employment opportunities in that region.
That is very clear. The purpose of this Bill, then, is to improve the economic lot of Atlantic Canadians.
What principles are embodied in the legislation? First, decisions are to be made in the region. Over 95 per cent of the decisions on direct assistance to business will be made in the region without reference to Ottawa. That process is now ongoing. The decentralization process is occurring and has occurred. Of a staff of about 300, only a small number, perhaps 20 or less, will be in Ottawa to participate in liaison and advocacy for the region.
What about consultation, another principle of this Bill? There is a 19 member board which will advise the Minister on policy. It will direct the staff, conduct studies and formulate new policy options. It will review program proposals and innovate unusual projects and will recommend policies or decisions to the Minister. That is flexibility. That is consultation.
By way of improving the business environment, under this legislation the agency will be able to provide more than direct assistance to business. It will be able to improve the opportunities in research, communication, co-operation and will provide scholarships related to business. The mechanism for federal-provincial co-operation are there. The co-financing mechanism is outlined. This will extend and enhance co-operation between government departments at the federal level and enhance cooperation with provincial departments.
Indeed, national programs will be directly impacted by regional needs to the advocacy program. The objective of the advocacy program is to promote an Atlantic perspective here in Ottawa to ensure that Atlantic Canada receives equitable consideration and benefits from national policies and programs. With respect to the specific goal of improving opportunities for medium and small business, the greatest number of ways and means, powers and authorities will be given to this agency so it will have the greatest flexibility to respond to the regions uniqueness.
I challenge the Opposition to tell us whether it is against these principles or does it support the idea of using a broad number of programs and a wide range of tools? Consultation has been lauded. In seeking more authority for the board, do Members opposite agree with decisions being taken in the region?
I have been disappointed as I sat through debate during the last few days not to hear the Opposition tell us whether it disagrees with the principles of this Bill. Instead it has complained about a wide range of things, many of them not based on fact. I challenge the Opposition to tell us whether it disagrees with the principles I have outlined.
In fact, just to comment on one of the suggestions of the Opposition about funding, it is clear that under our Government regional development spending has increased significantly. Under this program an additional $1 billion of new money will be made available to enhance economic development in our region. That is not money taken from other departments as has been suggested. It is new money. The programs that were in place in 1985 in my riding are still there. They are being funded. In addition to that, my constituents have the benefit of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and this new funding.
The suggestion that infrastructure funding is not possible is simply not based on any reading of the statute. The Minister of
January 21, 1988

Transport (Mr. Crosbie) was very clear in the House earlier this week when he said there are ERDA agreements, federal-provincial agreements, under which such arrangements can be concluded. None of that has changed. I believe we must move this Bill quickly into committee so that it can be made into law.
It is shameful that three days have been expended on a debate which does not concern the principles of this Bill. The debate has been about matters which can very well be addressed in committee. 1 have listened with interest to a lot of speculation from opposition Members about how this agency is going to work and where it is going to get its money and whether it can be successful. I have the distinct advantage of telling those Members that what we have in this legislation is not entirely new. The principles reflected in this legislation have been operating in Cape Breton for a couple of years through the Enterprise Cape Breton Agency. The principles of decentralization, the principles of autonomy and the principles of flexibility have been operating in Cape Breton. We have had a local board of directors with direct contact and accountability to a Minister. We have had a very successful two years.
In the last 12 months alone the unemployment rate in Cape Breton has dropped from 21 per cent to the area of 15 per cent or 16 per cent. That is real progress. That is proof that the economic regional development strategies of this Government can work and in fact are working. That I suggest is one of the reasons these principles are in the Bill. We know they can yield results which have alluded our regions for many decades.
That is not to say that all our problems will be solved quickly. However, it is to say that this is something better. This is progress. Maritimers and Atlantic Canadians are realistic. Anyone who stands before them and suggests that these problems will be solved overnight will not have credibility. Those who stand before Atlantic Canadians and say we believe this is in mechanism that will achieve progress, and then point to an example where progress has in fact happened, will have credibility. We have waited a long time for progress. We know that substantial and long term change takes time.
There has been the suggestion by some members of the Opposition that national economic progress is somehow irrelevant in Atlantic Canada. They have suggested that lower interest rates achieved as a result of better national management are irrelevant to Atlantic Canadians. Nothing could be further from the truth. My constituents buy homes, cars and furniture. Many of them borrow money to do so. They pay interest on that money. When interest rates are at 20 per cent they do not buy these goods, or else they pay a great deal more for them. We now have lower interest rates as a result of improved economic management. My constituents are saving money now.
There are small business people and prospective entrepreneurs as well in my riding. These people benefit from lower
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
interest rates. They can expand or initiate new business enterprises. Thus the argument that lower interest rates are somehow irrelevant in Atlantic Canada is not true. It is an illogical argument. It shows a total lack of understanding of the economy of Atlantic Canada.
What about lower inflation? Many of the same points can be made. When prices are rising that means there is less money to spend in a region such as Atlantic Canada. Where people have a lower income level, as is the case in Atlantic Canada, it amounts to just that much more. As a result of the improved management of the economy our Government has brought this benefit to Atlantic Canadians.
What about the deficit? The suggestion has been made that somehow controlling the deficit is contrary to the interests of Atlantic Canada. We pay taxes in Atlantic Canada. A large percentage of our taxes is used to serve the growing national debt. This means that there cannot be more money for better programs, whether they be social programs or regional development programs. The political Parties which advocate reckless and uncontrolled spending do a great disservice to those who strongly believe in regional development and in our social programs.
What about the lower unemployment rate? It was suggested today that unemployment is down only in Toronto. That is simply not true. Unemployment is down in Nova Scotia. In fact, the unemployment rate in Nova Scotia today is less than what the national unemployment rate was in 1984 when we were elected. What the previous Government would have given for the unemployment rate that we have in Nova Scotia today, Madam Speaker.
There are now more jobs in Atlantic Canada. We have a stronger economy. National economic growth is providing opportunities in the regions as well. There are people in the regions who want to leave, to go to the bigger centres where there are different economic opportunities than in the smaller centres. However, if there are no opportunities in the bigger centres then, obviously, they will not go to them. If we want to support our social programs we need economic growth.
The NDP talks so much about the regions. It was the New Democratic Party which sponsored and supported the national economic program that devastated the western region of our country. Today, the same Party stands just as firmly against free trade as it stood for the National Energy Program. It stands against-

COST OF STRIKES AND LOCK-OUTS-CALL FOR CHANGE IN RULES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, an objective look at strikes and lock-outs indicates that the real losers are third parties, the innocent people. For example, during the postal strike a small business went bankrupt because it could not deliver its products. Such losses could be multiplied hundreds of times.

REPORTED SMUGGLING OF CIGARETTES AND DRUGS THROUGH ST. REGIS INDIAN RESERVE

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to express my dissatisfaction with the Government's lack of action in dealing with the cigarette and drug smuggling occurring at the St. Regis Reserve in Cornwall, Ontario. subtopic: RECOMMENDATION THAT GOVERNMENT IMPLEMENT LABOUR RELATIONS SYSTEM TO MAINTAIN PEACE IN POST OFFICES AND IMPROVE SERVICES
RECOMMENDATION THAT GOVERNMENT IMPLEMENT LABOUR RELATIONS SYSTEM TO MAINTAIN PEACE IN POST OFFICES AND IMPROVE SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada Post Corporation was created, among other things, to improve labour relations. Canada Post made it its policy, in April 1987, to suspend any employee for three days the first time he or she forgets to punch his or her time card and for five days with possible dismissal the second time.
Mr. Speaker, the private sector does not go that far. Such an action, such a policy is an act of confrontation. Canada Post Corporation, with the agreement of the Conservative Government, is pursuing a policy of confrontation and, ultimately, Canadians will have to pay for a poorer service that deteriorates every day.
I ask the Conservative Government to forbid Canada Post Corporation from harassing its employees and to institute a labour relations system that will bring peace in post offices and give us a good postal service.

subsubtopic: MINISTER'S INFRACTION OF PROVISIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question would be better directed to the Prime Minister, but I think I can ask the Deputy Prime Minister to answer it. On September 25, 1985, the Minister of Energy, who at the time was Minister of Communications, left the Cabinet because he was under investigation for possible infractions of the Canada Elections Act. The Minister rose in the House of Commons at that time and said:
I am convinced that on completion of the investigation, my innocence will be established.
On November 28, Canada's Election Commissioner wrote to the Minister saying:
Proof in the dossier demonstrates that you participated in an infraction again Paragraph 62.6-
-of the Elections Act. Three days after the Minister received that letter telling him that he had violated the Canada Elections Act, the Prime Minister put him back into the Cabinet.

January 21, 1988

Member chooses to go along a certain line, that may be resented by some other Hon. Members. Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. Just by way of background, Your Honour and I were elected at the same time, and you will recall that in the early days of our time in this House it was common practice during all periods of

parliamentary debate, including Question Period, for Hon, Members to rise on points of order and questions of privilege if they felt that a question, comment or statement was in fact contrary to the rules as set out in the Standing Orders or in Beauchesne's. That practice carries on during debate now and the Chair does not always respond to every obvious violation of Standing Orders or practices of Beauchesne's, but the Chair certainly listens if someone rises on a point of order or a question of privilege in relation to a statement made, and the Chair reacts to that.
Because of the time that was taken up during Question Period with points of order and questions of privilege, the House decided, with agreement on both sides, that we would no longer permit points of order and questions of privilege during Question Period. That created a dilemma, 1 believe, and has over time caused the practices of the House in Question Period to change, not so much by deliberate choice or by decision of the House that this is the way we should go, but rather by the fact that there was then missing an opportunity to identify on a timely basis changes in procedures, questions and responses that may not have been in keeping with the practices as set out in the Standing Orders or in Beauchesne's.
I do not want to go into the details of the matter. I was of the opinion that parts of the questions raised by the Leader of the New Democratic Party were out of order simply because they asked a question of the Government that was beyond the Government's competence. I would have to read the "blues", but they were something to the effect of why the Commissioner of Elections took such and such an action. That is clearly beyond our competence. Had that been asked in normal debate or prior to the change in rules I would have been on my feet to say, on a point of order, that that question was out of order. The Chair could have agreed or disagreed with me at that point. My point is that through practice there have been no opportunities for Members on either side to raise those kinds of things.
I welcomed in your response to the Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker), Mr. Speaker, the indication that the Chair welcomes these kinds of observations and that, should Members believe that certain questions are out of order at any time, the House need not assume that each and every question has been carefully considered by the Chair and should be assumed to be in order unless the Chair ruled them out of order. In fact, the Chair welcomes observations about their appropriateness, propriety, and so on, and would take them into account.

I believe it is Citation 359 of Beauchesne's which describes the kind of questions that are allowed, which bears no relationship to what happens here now. I am not sure that it is the result of a carefully thought out decision on anyone's part what we want this place to become and how we want to project to the public that sent us here. Rather, 1 think it has arisen in part because of the inability, through the changes we made, to have
Privilege-Mr. Fulton
an opportunity for discussion on both sides to determine what is appropriate demeanour, response, and so on.
I welcome the opportunity to have this debate. I think we would do greater service to the public if we were a little more careful sometimes, if we had the opportunity to examine what we were doing, and if we exercised better judgment. I hope f am not being unfair, but too often it seems that it is the demands of the ten o'clock and eleven o'clock news which dictate behaviour in this Chamber rather than what we as parliamentarians in our heart of hearts would like to see this Chamber do.

subtopic: COMMITTEE ON ABORIGINAL AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT-REQUIREMENT FOR COMMITTEE TO REPORT
COMMITTEE ON ABORIGINAL AFFAIRS AND NORTHERN DEVELOPMENT-REQUIREMENT FOR COMMITTEE TO REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the issue is a little bit complicated. 1 will try to give you some idea as quickly as possible of from where the question of privilege flows.
A Bill known as Bill C-31 was passed by the House on June 12, 1985. Clause 22 of that Bill has two requirements, the first one being that the Minister shall cause to be laid before each House of Parliament, not later than two years after the Act is assented to, a series of items of information in relation to Bill C-31, including the number of people involved, the names and number of bands, and the impact of amendments on the lands and resources of the bands.
My question of privilege does not flow directly from that clause but from subclause (2) which says:
Such committee of Parliament as may be designated or established for the purposes of this subsection shall-
-not "may", but "shall"-"forthwith"-and its "forthwith", not "sometime in the distant future"-
-further on after the report of the Minister is tabled under subsection (1), review that report and may, in the course of that review, undertake a review of any provision of the Indian Act enacted by this Act.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) did table a report in June, 1987, as was required. There was a rather lengthy debate, as you might recall, in this House as a result of the fact that there was almost no information in the report. However, that is a debatable point.

January 21, 1988
Privilege-Mr. Fulton
The point I want to get to is that the committee of Parliament, which has been designated by this House as the Committee on Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development, shall report forthwith. That report has been before the Standing Commmittee on Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development since June, 1987. In various areas and bodies of law in the country there are definitions of what "forthwith" means. In some areas of law it can mean a few days. In other areas it means other things. To Parliament, obviously, it means the requirement to move with some kind of speed.
The difficulty is that last year there was a Chair appointed by the Government for the committee on aboriginal affairs but the committee was not called for nine calendar months last year. No witnesses were heard and no business was undertaken. I am not certain what could possibly have gone on to cause the committee not to sit.
However, last fall I was appointed to the Committee on Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development and am the permanent member of it. A steering committee meeting was held and a new Chair was chosen. As my colleague, the Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), and I have said on the record to the Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil), we were prepared to call it a new day in the committee and try to get the committee going. We began to invite witnesses in relation to Bill C-31 as we have a statutory responsibility to do. We invited the Assembly of First Nations, the Prairie Treaty Nations Alliance, and the Native Council of Canada, and we started moving on with other groups of witnesses.
Just before the break a committee meeting was held and a decision was taken there by motion and vote to call Mr. Justice E. Davey Fulton before the committee in February in relation to the Lubicon Indian band. The clerk of the committee was in touch with Mr. Fulton and he agreed to come on February 9. A very cordial and businesslike meeting of the committee was held with regard to the calling of other witnesses.
It was decided by all three Parties which were represented there that, because of the large number of witnesses-the Native Women's Association, and various bands, tribal councils and groups from across the country-who wanted to come, the job should be left to the staff and the clerk of the committee to request the presence of those witnesses on certain days beginning on Tuesday of this week for a full day of hearings and today for a full day of hearings.
The concern that I have, Mr. Speaker, is that without any notice or any attempt to give you notice by phone or mail, through the clerk or by any other means, the Chair of the committee cancelled all of those witnesses and all of those committee meetings. In some situations this might be seen only as an unfortunate situation, but this appears to be a conscious design in that once the committee stopped sitting last year it never sat again. It did not sit week after week until it had gone
for nine months without sitting. The only committee of Parliament that did not sit during those months was the Committee on Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development.
The concern that I have is that members of that committee at the very least, if not all Members of the House, are in some way, albeit in a grey area, in breach of the law. I direct you, Mr. Speaker, to look at Clause 16 which comes just before Clause 22, which says that should an aboriginal Canadian, Indian, Inuit, or Metis, violate any clause of Bill C-31 they are liable to extensive fines and up to six months' imprisonment. There are jail terms and fines for any aboriginal person who contravenes any clause of this Act, but neither the Minister nor the committee has done what is required by the law.
It seems to me that there is an intentional blockage of the committee. I came here with my schedule prepared for a full day of hearings on Tuesday. I learned only yesterday, and confirmed it this morning, that all of the witnesses and all of the hearings were cancelled for today as well. This leads me to believe that members of the committee are in some way already in breach of Section 22(2). There must at some point be a definition of "forthwith". It surely cannot mean never. If saying that a parliamentary committee must report forthwith means that it never has to report, that is an interesting new definition of forthwith, albeit something which many aboriginal people have come to expect.
I have had calls from aboriginal groups who have been denied their right to appear as witnesses. It is starting to cast a shadow, and not only upon the Government. There are many aboriginal people who are extremely angry with the Government because of its policies. However, this is now casting a pall upon all Members.
My final point is that I have things to do in terms of serving my constituency. I arranged my time to be here for committees that were scheduled six weeks ago. On Monday of this week the Chair of the committee cancelled those for Tuesday. I am not sure when he cancelled the hearings for today.
I cannot arrange my calendar to the whim of a chairman who has never called me. He has been in the House every day but has never spoken to me or given me a note. At some point 1 think the Chair will have to rule on the meaning of "forthwith", whether we are in breach of the law, and at what point the cancelling or lack of holding of committee meetings reaches the privileges and reforms of the House. I am prepared to move a motion to move this entire matter before the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure, where I think it should best be resolved.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, your instructions regarding how we should approach this question of privilege are most helpful. Indeed, I will argue that there are such circumstances that do call for intervention from another authority.
All Hon. Members in the House will know that ordinarily, as Your Honour has suggested, committees are masters of their own arrangements. They control the manner and the rate in which they do their business. We could call that a precedent of the House of Commons. The committees are only subject to Standing Orders.
For example, if a committee refuses to meet, then it can invoke Standing Order 92(2), which states that four members may require a meeting. I will not go over that Standing Order and take up your time, but would just add that when there are only two opposition Members on a committee, Standing Order 92(2) very quickly becomes inoperative.
If we were to argue just that, we would be bringing to your attention something that could be called a grievance rather than a privilege and you would be quite correct in dismissing it forthwith.
However, the current situation with the Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Committee is really quite different.
I want to argue that at the present time the aboriginal affairs committee of the House is under the obligation of law to fulfil certain duties. Namely, it is to look at the impact of Bill C-31 and is required to report to Parliament as to what changes are necessary. It is a statutory obligation, laid upon the aboriginal affairs committee.
According to Beauchesne 4th Edition, Citation 13, page 12, whenever there is an expressed order of the House, whenever there is a statute or statute regulation, that supersedes every mere usage or precedent. Therefore, the concerns that you raised about whether we were just calling upon you to interfere with the operation of a committee, you can see immediately that we go well beyond that because we are under the obligation of the law.
Privilege-Mr. Fulton
The Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) and myself, as members of this committee, want very much to fulfil our statutory obligations. However, we believe that we are being prevented from doing so. When an Hon. Member is in any way prevented from carrying out his or her duties, then I would argue that this becomes a prima facie case of privilege.
Let me illustrate. Before the Christmas recess, it was agreed by all Members that we would allow the staff to do the scheduling, to call the witnesses and immediately upon resumption of Parliament, beginning this week of January 18, we would get down to work. Those witnesses were properly notified. They made their travel plans and were prepared to be here. Then, unilaterally, on his own volition, the Chairman cancelled all the meetings. All of those witnesses had to be notified not to come to Ottawa and they were inconvenienced and extremely angry and upset.
I think it could be argued that the Chairman is breaking the law. There is in the Criminal Code of Canada a very generalized penalty for breaking any statute. However, I will not argue that point at all because I would not want to tempt the Speaker to tell me to refer this matter to the Attorney General of Canada and have the matter delayed.
What we need is immediate action from Your Honour. If the chairman of the committee will not follow the law on his own volition, he must be directed to do so by someone who has authority over him. You, Sir, as the first among equals in this House, have that authority to order Members of Parliament to obey the law as that law impinges directly on them. Therefore, I am asking you to rule in favour of a question of privilege so that the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges and Procedure can fully review this matter and be empowered to issue very strict orders that the committee must meet and must report because the law requires it to do so.
Let me add another illustration. If the Auditor General of Canada did not carry out his important duties and report to Parliament, there would be an outcry. If the Public Accounts Committee did not meet to consider a report from the Auditor General, that would be a serious matter. It would be a grievance, but no law would be broken.
The Auditor General, however, must audit and the Auditor General must report. The law requires him to do so. He is under a statutory obligation.
Similarly in this case, 1 am arguing that the Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Committee does not just operate on its own will. It is under the obligation of Section 22(2) of an Act of Parliament under Bill C-31. It is operating under the law and must, therefore, meet forthwith.
The Hon. Member for Skeena indicated that the Minister for Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) reported on June 26, 1987. The aboriginal affairs commmittee did not have a single meeting on Bill C-31 until December 10 and the Statute says that it is to meet forthwith. How liberally can one interpret the term "forthwith"?

January 21, 1988
Business of the House
1 call upon you, Sir, to intervene in the name of the law and to get this committee working and operative so that its statutory obligations can be fulfilled.
