subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to speak on the Bill that is before us today. It has two principal sections in it, one being the establishment of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, and the other being the establishment of the Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation.
This is an interesting piece of legislation. We have seen this type of thing laid out before the House before. What is really behind it is what residents of Atlantic Canada would like to know more about. 1 say that because they certainly have been given a great deal of bluster and shell game by government Members, including a Minister who spoke this morning, as to what is really happening in terms of the Bill. We know roughly what kind of new or old money will be allocated. It is just over $1 billion over five years, that is, just over $200 million per year.
The Bill purports to be a new kind of decentralization. A special board will be created and so on. As I intend to point out, there is far less money than there used to be, either under
the present Government or under any other previous Government in terms of real dollars per capita for regional development in Atlantic Canada. There really is not the kind of decentralization that government Members herald this measure to be.
I think a great many Atlantic Canadians would like to know what is really happening in terms of job creation in Canada, what free trade will mean and what these two new agencies will mean in terms of economic development, and whether or not small and medium-sized businesses, to which they are supposedly targeted, are the ones which will really benefit. We have to do a bit of looking to see whether or not what the Government is telling the people of Atlantic Canada is in fact what will happen. That is the proper role of MPs, whether they be government Members or opposition Members. It is certainly the role of opposition Members.
Statistics were released last year with respect to where jobs were being created in Canada. Such was reported on February 28, 1987, in The Globe and Mail. It was stated in an article in that newspaper that day that between January, 1986, and January, 1987, the total number of jobs in the country rose by 137,000, according to unadjusted figures, but only 5,000 of those jobs were created outside of Ontario. That certainly was and is well known in western Canada, which is where I come from. 1 come from an area not terribly different from some parts of Newfoundland, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, or certainly some areas of the Province of Quebec, if we include some of its areas as having the type of employment difficulties that are found in much of rural, northern and maritime Canada.
The games that can be played with figures are many. We heard the Minister and various Members from the government side claiming that this is new money and that it is more money. They said that it would really be the initiative that would finally get Atlantic Canada's economy going. Then, on March 7, 1987, not too long after this article pointing out where jobs were really being created was printed, it was pointed out that it is those regions of the country where we are starting to find real sluggishness in the economy. We see that in the areas of the country where the economy is really at work there is no unemployment. 1 refer to Toronto and the Golden Horseshoe, or the Golden Triangle, or whatever one calls it depending on what part of the country one lives in.
Many Atlantic Canadians were interested when the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) said that the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency may be the last kick at the can as far as development programs for the region from the federal Government are concerned. He went on to say, "I think it will work but it may be the last kick at the can from what the federal Government may do in the region". What does the Minister of Public Works mean? I think we have to look at some figures to find out just exactly what this means.
We can look at some federal Government figures to give us some idea of why this is really a shell game, that these are not
January 21, 1988

new dollars or that this is not some kind of a great new initiative. In the regional development envelope, between the time the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) took office and now, there has been a reduction of $2.89 billion between fiscal 1984-85 and fiscal 1987-88. That figure will certainly rise to well beyond $3 billion by the time we end this fiscal year. There were cuts in the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion to the tune of $200 million in the first year the Conservative Government was in office. Some $100 million more was cut from the Department in 1985-86, while $150 million was cut from the Department last year. There have been all kinds of other cuts to the regional economy of Atlantic Canada. Some $16 million was cut from the East Coast ferry services. There was $100 million cut in Cape Breton alone in relation to the 700 jobs that were lost at the heavy water plants. The estimate, which is clearly accurate and perhaps even on the conservative side, is that on an annual basis since the election of the present Government there has been a cut in federal spending in the Atlantic region of $1 billion.
If we take a look at the figures we will see that there is around $200 million per year being proposed under these agencies being set up in Atlantic Canada with these boards having anywhere from up to 20 members. While $1 billion is being cut, $200 million is being replaced. This, of course, is something that Governments are embarrassed to admit, rather than announcing their plans year by year and saying, "We are taking $800 million away and we are giving you $200 million". A great many Governments forget that those dollars come from the people of Atlantic Canada. They come from Canadians. They are not printed solely here in Ottawa by Governments as they come and go from power.
What is happening is that the Government, rather than announcing the initiative province by province, a few million here and a few million there per year, adds all the provinces together and then multiplies by five. Why does it not multiply by 10? My colleagues have touched on this before. Why does it not multiply by 20, 30, or 40 to make it sound like some substantial amount of money? Certainly Atlantic Canadians and Canadians I represent in the most western constituency of Canada do not forget very quickly that this is the Government that, on a quick, late evening phone call signed a cheque and gave a $500 million gift to the Reichmann brothers in Toronto to help them along with their Gulf deal. They like to call it a tax break-the Little Egypt Bump-they do not like to admit that it is gift wrapped. Those are real dollars. They are not 50 cent or 80 cent dollars. The $500 million that was given to the Reichmanns was real Canadian taxpayers' dollars. Of course, there was the billion for the bank bail-out, and the billion for the bail-out of bad loans that banks had offshore. There is lots of money to be spent out of Ottawa, but the priorities of the Conservative Government are what have to be looked at. Those two agencies are being sold very much as a pig in a poke to Atlantic Canadians.
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
We have to take a look at what the Government has been saying this really is. They claim that it is decentralized control over regional development. Many Atlantic Canadians found there was too much bureaucracy, it was too difficult to get through to Ottawa, it was too difficult to find out what the programs were, and it tended to be seen very much more as a straight patronage oriented operation whenever money was spent.
Senator Lowell Murray, the Minister responsible for the new agency, ACOA, was reported in the Globe and Mail on June 27, 1987 as saying that final decisions will be made by him in Ottawa. "The ultimate responsibility rests with me," and a Cabinet committee made up of the six federal Ministers from the Atlantic region.
The Bill claims that the decisions are being put into the hands of some Atlantic Canadians from various areas of Atlantic Canada and that they are going to make the decisions. But we find that just as the Government does not want to give as much money as it is taking away, it also does not want to give the type of decentralized decision-making that it claims this Bill is all about.
The power of the Minister and the lack of autonomy of the agency is clearly articulated. Anyone who wishes to read it will find it in Clauses 5, 6, 7, and 20, that is regarding the role and powers of the Minister. Clause 11 reveals the ties that the President of the agency has with the Minister in that the President is the deputy of the Minister and is "under the direction of the Minister".
It is worth taking a moment to take a look at what has generally happened over the years with the commitments from Ottawa regardless of Government, and we find that there has been a decline. Over the last 25 years less than 3 per cent of total federal economic expenditures have been applied to regional development. That is a statement that 1 feel very much involved in, in terms of what types of money is actually returned to the north coast.
We have a salmon industry that is worth $750 million a year. Huge amounts of taxes are paid on that. We have Prince Rupert Grain operating once again. As a matter of fact, it started moving grain only a couple of hours ago. A very substantia! amount of revenue is created and generated for farmers across the country as a result of the operation of that grain elevator, or Ridley Terminals, for the movement of northeast coal from northeastern British Columbia, Tumbler Ridge, and so on down and out through Prince Rupert.
I know how rarely it is that federal economic development moneys make it out to the distant regions of the country, whether it is in the forest sector, in relation to new technology, research and development for sawmills and so on; whether it is in the fishery sector, in the mining sector, or in generalized small and medium sized businesses. That is why all Canadians, not only Atlantic Canadians, should take a close look at what type of legislation this Government is bringing forward.

January 21, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
It is clearly a pre-election period. We see the Prime Minister trying to live up to his promises that his Government would double the amount spent on research and development. He is never going to make it, but at least he is attempting to live up to some promises. There is the western development initiative, the Atlantic initiative, the northern Ontario initiative. There will be more initiatives between now and the election. They will always be for large areas and for many years or multiples of years, for five or ten years, to make the amount budgeted sound very large, whereas in fact the early years of expenditure are almost always very small. It is a political expediency and trickery that Canadians who live in the regions have come to expect not only of the Conservative Government but very much of the Trudeau years.
Explicit regional development expenditures in 1984-85 for all of Atlantic Canada were in the order of $230 million. We also have to weigh that. Many Atlantic Canadians or members of their families spend part of the year collecting unemployment insurance because of their seasonal employment, whether it is in the lobster fishery, the cod fishery, as shore workers, in the forest sector, or in small business or tourism. But the $230 million that this Government felt was appropriate for regional development in Atlantic Canada is only 15 per cent of what is paid in unemployment insurance. We have to take a look at that. There was $1.6 billion coming out through unemployment insurance payments. The total amount that is going in for regional development is one-seventh of that amount. We have to start thinking about that in terms of how Government makes expenditures and what are its priorities.
Let us look at expenditures under DRIE's industrial incentive programs. They have decreased in real terms from $9 per person almost 20 years ago in the 1969-70 fiscal period to $4 under the Government. These are not inflation related dollars, they are 1981 dollars. There was $9 per person 20 years ago and it is $4 per person now. If that is a commitment to the small and medium-sized enterprises in Atlantic Canada, it is not much of a commitment to be as nice as one possibly can.
Comparing Newfoundland to the area I come from in the Queen Charlotte Islands where there is a lot of fishing, forestry, and similar types of occupations and similar types of unemployment found in the areas, for Newfoundland the reduction in the same period was from $9 per person to $3 per person, while expenditures under the general development agreements and economic and regional development agreements, known as GDAs and ERDAs, have declined from $16 per person 13 years ago to $14 under this Government in the 1984-88 period. We are seeing a decline in all of those areas whether one looks at it in terms of fixed dollars or in any other way.
For Newfoundland the reduction was from $126 per person to $80 per person, while Ontario experienced an increase from $2 to $3 per person. When comparing what is happening in the regions, we are seeing a real decline, whether it is measured
over 20 years, 10 years, 5 years, or however it is measured. There is a reduction in the amount of real dollars going out for economic development into the regions, whether we are talking about the Atlantic region, northern British Columbia, or other regions of the country, whereas in the area of the country where there is no real measurable unemployment, because most of those people are moving between jobs which are found when there is 5 per cent unemployment, as is found in the constituency of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson)-that is how low the unemployment is there-there is an increase.
My colleague from St. John's East (Mr. Harris) has kindly provided me with the most recent Statistics Canada unemployment rates in percentage. Last year in Newfoundland it was 18.6 per cent; in Prince Edward Island, 13.3; Nova Scotia, 12.5; New Brunswick, 13.2; Quebec, 10.3; Ontario, 6.1; Manitoba, 7.4; Saskatchewan, 7.3; Alberta, 9.6; and British Columbia, 12.0. We start getting some idea of what is happening in the country.
We heard from the Minister of State for Forestry another example of a promise made by the Prime Minister. There was going to be a full Ministry and Minister of Forestry as soon as the Government was elected. What did we get? We got a Minister of State for Forestry, who is very good at his job. I am not running him down for one moment. I think that he is very good at his job, and that is certainly what I hear from the sector. But we find that he has been buried. He has almost no staff, almost no Department, and to give him more work to do, mining was added on.
The regional occupations of a very substantial number of Canadians are in the forest sector. There are more than 1 million Canadians, if one takes those who are indirectly and directly employed in the forest sector. So we have a Minister of State with half a dozen senior staff, attempting to assist in terms of all the programs and everything that is going on. We know that the forest sector is running into some very difficult times as a result of bad management of the resource. There are too many companies cutting an ever diminishing number of mature and harvestable trees. In the mining sector again we see the Minister overloaded.
We have to ask why the Government would decide to try to confuse the voters of Atlantic Canada as to what is really being done. It cut the funds, then it announced a partial return, then that is multiplied by five and called a major new program, a major new initiative. Then the Minister of Pubic Works states that it is the "last kick at the can". If that is the way the Conservatives think they will catch the interest of Atlantic Canadians, I think they will find out soon enough that it is not acceptable.
The Bill will give ACOA control over federal regional development programs specifically related to the Atlantic
January 21, 1988

region-the Industrial and Regional Development Program, known as IRDP; the Atlantic Enterprise Program, known as AEP; the Small Businesses Loans Act as it relates to the region; IRDA subagreements in relation to forestry, tourism, and so on; and the Atlantic Development Program.
I think I have dealt with the key points that I wanted to cover in some detail. The Government has announced that it is the major and last initiative and that it is decentralization. 1 think 1 have demonstrated that it is the furthest thing from decentralization. In fact, as Senator Lowell Murray said, the control over this is remaining in his hands, and he is not even available for questioning in the House or from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux), the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), or any member of the Opposition. No one gets to question him because he is not a Member of Parliament. He is not responsible to anyone. He can make whatever kinds of decisions he wants. There has been no decentralization. In fact there has been a major chopping of money rather than the kind of topping up there should have been.
There is nothing in the legislation which specifically requires that jobs created are in any way to be considered fundamental to the awarding of ACOA funding. There is no targeting. In general terms it says that it is for small and medium-sized enterprises, but it does not include the rigid and precise kinds of definitions which provide results. Does a corporation have to create new jobs, or does it just have to create more profits? Can those profits be diverted elsewhere? There is a fundamental kind of language or targeting which can be included in Bills to allow Parliament and Atlantic Canadians to decide whether or not their money is being well spent.
I am sorry I do not have more time to speak today. There are all kinds of comments I would like to make about proposals which I think should be made for Atlantic Canada. Perhaps, if someone questioned me about that, I might take the opportunity to expound a little on what I think would be a better way of dealing with economic development initiatives in Atlantic Canada.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member what he has to say to the notion we heard in the House twice today, once from the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil)-and the Hon. Member was commenting on it when the lunch break came- and once from the Deputy Government House Leader, that for some reason we were wasting the time of the House talking about this very important issue.
It is an issue which affects four provinces of the country. It is a most important issue. In the context of the business of the House, speakers from our Party wish to raise their concerns about the issue and to point out how government has failed, not only this Government but the previous Government as well.
Is it any wonder that the following conclusion can be reached by economists? I draw the attention of the House to
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
the comments of Elizabeth Beale, a consulting economist for the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council. In the 1987 report she went back through 15 years of regional development programs of the Government of Canada, that is, this Government and the previous one. She says that there has been very little improvement in any of the major indicators of regional disparities between the Atlantic provinces and the country as a whole, and that the gap in unemployment rates is proportionately the same now as it was 15 years ago. She also indicates that although personal incomes have been raised slightly, the increase is attributable to the increase in personal transfer payments. She also says that funding for regional development efforts in recent years has been well below the peak reached in the late 1970s.
Is it any wonder-and I would like the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) to comment on this-that this is the case when the attention of the House cannot be directed to this issue for a period of four days or five days because the Deputy Government House Leader and a member of the government Party from Nova Scotia complain about the fact that we are talking about this issue on a national basis in the forum to which we were elected to debate issues of national importance? This is an issue of national importance. It is not only an issue of importance to Atlantic Canada.
I was pleased to see the Hon. Member for Skeena, whose riding is one of the farthest from my own, take the time to come to the House to speak on an issue of national importance. I would like to ask for his comments on that and for some suggestions he may have to improve regional development programs.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to take the opportunity to do that. I share the concern of the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. Harris) about the comments of the Government House Leader and the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) concerning three days of debate on Atlantic Canada. It is $1 billion for five years for all the provinces, so it is $200 million for a year"? What if he went on to say: "But that is not just for Nova Scotia. It is for the four provinces"? Even if it is evenly divided-and it will

January 21, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
not be-it will amount to $50 million each. Then if we break that down into 12 months, it comes to about $4 million. If we break it down further, it comes to a couple of bucks a day. There is not very much.
I know why the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands- Canso is embarrassed. It is because there is not much money going to Cape Breton, to Nova Scotia, or to New Brunswick. This is why the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew) was talking about things he used to do when he was in the provincial Cabinet. He had to talk about what they used to do 20 years ago. He did not want to talk about the money that is in there. He did not want to talk about the legislation. He was nervous. He was worried. He was paranoid. Those Tories have crowed the falsification for too long. I know why the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso did not come back for questions this afternoon. It was because I caught him being mischievous at the very best. He was saying that the NDP had supported the National Energy Program in western Canada. Tories from Alberta have loved to crow about that in every election. They have said that members of the NDP were supporters of the National Energy Program and that they destroyed the economy of western Canada. There are many western Canadians who know that that is a lot of bumf. Tories can go around and talk about it, but all they need to do is to look at the public record to see that we did not vote with the Liberals. We voted with the Tories. Is that not amazing? We opposed the National Energy Program. However, it makes good grist in rural ridings which have small newspapers. They can manage to get these stories out and move them around.
This is why government Members do not want this stuff debated. The media in Atlantic Canada are starting to pick up on it. They are starting to say: "Just a minute". They gave glowing coverage to this $1.05 billion. The Prime Minister got his shoulder to it and just managed to squeeze it over the $1 billion mark. He might as well have said that it was over six years rather than $1.05 billion over five years.
Why not tell the truth to each province? Why not tell Nova Scotia that it is only $20 million? We do not know how it will break down. What we do know is that it is controlled by Senator Lowell Murray who cannot be questioned by anybody in this place or by anyone in Atlantic Canada. He certainly is not responsible to this board. It is a remarkable state of affairs.
The Hon. Member for St. John's East says that it is good that I am involved in the debate. I feel good about being involved in the debate because I have been to Newfoundland and I know what problems are faced by Newfoundlanders. I have been to Nova Scotia. 1 have been to New Brunswick. 1 have been to P.E.I. I have been in the Province of Quebec. I have been in all Maritime and Atlantic areas, and the problems which are faced there are very similar to those in northwestern British Columbia. I represent an area which is almost the size of France, and it will be bigger in the next election. The Government thought: "give him something bigger to represent and maybe that will keep him quiet". Of course it will not. It will really get my blood pumping.
The Hon. Member for St. John's East referred to an important point which has been raised by a number of economists in Atlantic Canada. As I am sure he would know- and in fact he used it in his own speech-the Economic Council of Canada, in its report released on September 30, 1987, indicated that the issue of economic disparity, particularly regional economic disparity, will be the largest problem facing the country over the next five years. It said the national economy is likely to expand steadily in coming years but uneven regional growth will be the country's major economic problem. Does the Government respond? No. It sends $500 million in Loomis trucks down to the Reichmann Brothers in Toronto. It is sending $1 billion to the banks to pay off bad loans they made outside of Canada. It is sending $1 billion to bail out some of its pals in the banking industry out west. Yet what does it give for the whole of Atlantic Canada? Is it even as much as the Reichmann Brothers got in one present in 1987? No. It gives $200 million per year to the whole of Atlantic Canada.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-103, an Act to increase opportunity for economic development in Atlantic Canada, to establish the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and Enterprise Cape Breton Corporation and to make consequential and related amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, ATLANTIC CANADA, 1987 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am happy to have an opportunity to speak this afternoon on Bill C-103. I know of the serious financial and economic difficulties which have been facing Atlantic Canada for many years. Even though when they joined Confederation they were one of the richest areas in the country, they have now suffered greatly. This Bill is designed to do something in that regard.
However, we are worried that it will be very similar to the northern Ontario recovery program which the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) talked about in the fall of 1986. He told us then that because of the slow economic growth in northern Ontario, which is very similar to Atlantic Canada, he was considering a number of options. They included a federal
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
economic development committee, and a transfer of some federal agencies and services to northern Ontario. Project moneys were going to be dedicated to northern Ontario. A stabilization program was going to be established for the forest and mining industries. Special tax treatment was going to be given to equity investors in the region.
It is interesting to note that even though the Deputy Prime Minister said that on November 19, 1986, none of that has come to pass. Nothing has really happened. Something seemed to have happened last July. There was a grand announcement that the Government was establishing the Fednor program. It was going to establish a committee. Yet seven months later the program is not operational. You cannot find out by phoning any government office in Sudbury or Sault Ste. Marie or Thunder Bay what the criteria is for that program. Supposedly it will eventually provide some $8 million a year in loans or grants. Yet you cannot find out what that program will cover. Does it cover small business or large business? Does it cover manufacturing and processing or the service industry or transportation or whatever? We do not know. From what I have heard during this debate, ACOA does not know exactly what is going to be covered or how it will work.
I have a suspicion that even though the Fednor program for northern Ontario was announced by the Solicitor General and the Minister for Regional Industrial Expansion last July 13, there was absolutely no money allocated for the fiscal year 1987-88. If not, then of course the whole thing is really a charade.
What other reason can there be for indicating that the Government wants to start a program like this in the fall of 1986 and 16 months have gone by and the application forms do not exist? The criteria for the program does not exist. There is only one very small aspect of the whole program even available. There is talk in the Deputy Prime Minister's statement about a stabilization program for forestry and mining. What a joke. Two months after the Minister made that statement in the House, the Government imposed an export tax of 15 per cent on the forest industry. Do you think that will stabilize the industry? In fact, it cost northern Ontario some $26 million in 1987 to stay in the softwood lumber exporting industry. Fortunately, because of a very strong market in the U.S., the industry has survived. However, as the market turns down in 1988, as many economic forecasters indicate it will, that export tax will be devastating to the industry.
There is another little hook here. The Ontario Government chose not to transfer that export tax to a stumpage charge. If it did, the amount could be twice the $25 million. I am surprised that any company in the softwood industry in northern Ontario could pay a tax of that magnitude and still survive. Clearly, if it is transferred to a stumpage charge, it will be that much more devastating.

January 21, 1988
Government Organization Act, Atlantic Canada, 1987
The Deputy Prime Minister talked about a stabilization program for the mining industry. Six months after he said that, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) came into the House with a tax reform Bill which does away with flowthrough shares and the earned depletion allowance. That mechanism generated this year some $500 million or $600 million for mining exploration and development along the Lake Superior shore and the area North of Sudbury and across the north channel area. Exploration and development is now taking place, but it will not be when that program is phased out next year.
There is a whole series of assaults on northern Ontario at a time when the Government is talking glibly about a northern Ontario recovery program. 1 am sure the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency will face the same kind of assaults. So many of the areas of Canada which have not been doing very well since the economic recession of 1981 have suffered difficulties from slow growth.
The other aspect mentioned by the Deputy Prime Minister in November of 1986 was the transferring of whole government Departments to regions like northern Ontario. Yet looking at the facts, we see that some 1,300 jobs have actually been moved out of northern Ontario. Practically every government Department, whether it be the Post Office, Indian Affairs, Employment and Immigration or the Armed Forces, has been moved out. As well, another 500 people have been laid off as a result of the export tax which caused many of the softwood lumber and stud mills to be shut down.
There is almost a conspiracy against slow growth areas like northern Ontario at a time when the Government is talking about recovery programs. I am sure that Atlantic Canadians are facing the same difficulties. My concern is that we do not simply pick out of the air nice, glib names like northern Ontario recovery program or Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency without actually putting money into these areas where so many other economic factors apply.
This afternoon, 1 heard the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines (Mr. Merrithew) say how wonderful free trade would be for the Province of New Brunswick. However, it was only two weeks ago that Harrison McCain of McCain Foods, one of the largest food processing companies in Canada, said on a Sunday morning news magazine that the whole free trade arrangement which would remove tariffs on processed foods but maintain marketing boards will simply not work. He said that there will be only two choices for the grocery manufacturing industry to make: to destroy the marketing boards for poultry, turkeys, eggs and dairy products, marketing boards which the Government is trying to maintain, or to move processing plants to the United States.
Mr. McCain said that he could live with it either way. He said that he had plants operating in the United States as well as plants operating in Canada. He would prefer to continue to supply the Canadian market from his plants in Canada, but if
the Government chooses to go ahead with the free trade agreement, he will simply operate the plants in the United States and ship the food into Canada.
1 believe that that is one of the least understood aspects of the free trade deal. The grocery manufacturing sector is the largest manufacturing sector in Canada. Gross volumes of sales amount to some $40 billion per year. The sector employs
225,000	people, more than the total number of farmers in Canada who are making above the economic minimum of $20,000 in gross revenues.
The free trade agreement will increase quotas for poultry, meat, eggs and turkeys and will remove tariffs on processed food coming into Canada. Eventually, there will be a confrontation. It might not happen for two or three years, but eventually the grocery manufacturers of Canada who employ a great many people and have a massive volume of business will put it to the Government that it will have to either get rid of the farm marketing boards or they will move their plants and operations to the United States. I predict that at that stage, the marketing boards will be destroyed.
I listened to the Minister of State for Forestry and Mines and I have a great deal of respect for his remarks on most issues. However, I do not think he has looked into the problems of the grocery manufacturers in his own Province of New Brunswick or in the rest of Atlantic Canada.
We have to talk not only about pro-active programs like the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency but we have to look at all those underlying government programs which have been cut back. Services to farm groups like the inspection of potatoes have been cut back. More and more costs are being loaded on the input side. We must look at the cost of assistance provided in transportation agencies and the fishery as well as high profile programs. After all, a few million dollars in incentives often go a long way.
I have been very impressed with the small business economic development corporations which have been set up in my own constituency under the Department of Employment and Immigration. They have been extremely effective in creating jobs, often much more effective than the programs run by DRIE. One aspect of that program has been the involvement of local committees, and I think that is a very worth-while part of any economic development program including the one before us here today.
Those are some of my concerns. I am concerned that we do not take away jobs and that we do not impose new taxation as was the case with softwood lumber and the removal of the earned depletion allowance and flow-through shares. All government programs should be co-ordinated.
I want to see the Government not only announce and talk about these things but put the money up to see that these programs actually work and are not just a charade that will have no effect on balancing economic opportunities for the

slow-growth areas of Canada, the North and the eastern provinces.
