subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT ADVISABILITY OF INTENSIFYING RESEARCH FOR ALTERNATIVES TO REFRIGERANTS
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT ADVISABILITY OF INTENSIFYING RESEARCH FOR ALTERNATIVES TO REFRIGERANTS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of intensifying research for alternatives to refrigerants such as freon, which contain chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) that erode the earth's ozone layer.
He said: Madam Speaker, I will proceed quickly to explain the reason for this motion. The use of chlorofluorocarbons, which are commonly described as CFCs is based on the fact that they are propellants in aerosols such as hairsprays, deodorants and anti-perspirants. This use was banned in 1980, yet clorofluorocarbons are still used as propellants for cooking and paint sprays.
The most common use for chlorofluorocarbons is as a coolant in refrigerators, freezers and air conditioning units. These clorofluorocarbons to which I will refer as CFCs are also used extensively in foams, including rigid insulation foam, flexible foam for cushions and foam for packaging food.
The high-tech and communications industries use certain forms of CFCs as a solvent for cleaning electrical circuits and
the like. It should be pointed out that Canada is a small player in the clorofluorocarbon game, using only 22,000 of the estimated 940,000 tonnes per year consumed the world over. In the United States, for instance, 90 per cent of cars sold have air conditioning, as do 80 per cent of light trucks. This market alone consumes 54,000 tonnes of CFC 12 as a coolant, which is more than twice Canadian consumption of all chlorofluorocarbons.
One may wonder why refrigerants are named in this motion. It is because this is the largest of all the chlorofluorocarbons uses in Canada. Some 9,000 of the 22,000 tonnes of chlorofluorocarbons consumed annually in Canada are for refrigeration purposes.
What threat do chlorofluorocarbons pose? The five commonly used CFCs, namely, 11, 12, 113, 114 and 115, erode the ozone layer in the stratosphere, some 20 to 40 kilometres above the earth. Chlorofluorocabons are gaseous and travel easily in the atmosphere. They do not break down easily in the lower atmosphere and can last from 60 to 300 years in the stratosphere.
The ozone acts as the earth's sunscreen. It blocks some of the sun's ultraviolet radiation from reaching the earth's surface. What would happen if the amount of ultraviolet radiation increased? Health would be affected. Scientists in Environment Canada and elsewhere predict that the number of cases of skin cancer and eye cataracts would increase.
Our immune system would also be affected and even suppressed, making people even more susceptible to certain diseases, viruses and infections. The environment would be affected. Scientists predict that agricultural crops would not grow as well or yield as much, and that phytoplankton, the basis of the food chain in the oceans, would be adversely affected. The air quality would also be in question because ultraviolet radiation is a contributor to smog in urban areas. Therefore, an increase in ultraviolet radiation would create more smog and more associated health problems such as eye and nose irritation and, more important, asthma and heart problems.
This brings me to the global warming question, which is an issue that has been more recently raised in scientific circles and through the media for public consideration, chlorofluorocarbons also contribute to the greenhouse effect of global warming.
We mostly hear about carbon dioxide emitted by burning coal, oil, wood and gas as being the main culprit of global warming. However, C02 pales in comparison to CFCs. Scientists estimate that a molecule of CFC is 10,000 times more effective than a molecule of C02 in absorbing and radiating infra-red radiation, the process which warms up the atmosphere. Today it is estimated that CFCs account for about 10 per cent to 15 per cent of the warming trend. If CFCs continue to travel into the atmosphere at the present rate, that could grow to 50 per cent in 50 years.
January 21, 1988

There has been a global response to this question of ozone depletion and damage. In September, 1987, the United Nations Environment Program sponsored a protocol on substances that deplete the ozone layer. It was signed in Montreal by 24 nations and the European Economic Community. If it were ratified and implemented, it would reduce the global consumption of the five ozone-depleting CFCs to 50 per cent of the production level of 1986 by the year 1998. This is a tremendous step forward.
Elowever, we should not rest on our laurels. Due to the long life of CFCs in the stratosphere-60 to 300 years-Environment Canada suggested that a reduction of 85 per cent is required in order just to stabilize the levels of ozone in the atmosphere. This view is endorsed by many environmental groups and organizations, such as the Nordic Environmental Ministers, who advocate complete elimination as soon as possible.
Therefore, it would make sense to urge our Government to ratify the protocol immediately, to formulate and publish a strategy for reducing to zero our consumption of chlorofluorocarbon in the shortest possible time, and to launch a global initiative with like-minded Governments with the aim of eliminating rather than reducing by 50 per cent the production of ozone-depleting chlorofluorocarbons.
This is also a terrific opportunity for parliamentarians. The effort to sustain ourselves on this planet can also be moved on the international agenda. For example, those Members who are members of the Inter-Parlimentary Union which is scheduled to meet in Guatemala next April, can talk about sustainable development because it is on the agenda and will be debated there.
The Government of Canada also has a role to play. It could intensify its research effort in areas such as monitoring the progress and effort of the industry in research endeavours. It could ensure the transfer of new technology and information to Canadian users, consumers and importers of CFCs and products containing chlorofluorocarbons.
It should intensify its research in non CFC solutions, including the use of helium or other refrigerants, new designs for refrigerator systems, or other replacement technologies such as the solar powered refrigerator invented by a Guelph engineer. The fridge has no moving parts, no compressor and, most important, no CFC refrigerant.
It should study methods and technologies for the conversion of CFC-based processes to non-CFC systems. This is an important area in which to intensify research and promoting efforts.
It is also important to develop intensive co-operation with Canadian industry on demonstration projects and to develop methods and technologies for the conversion of chlorofluorocarbons based processes to non-CFC systems.
Finally, we must search for ways to reduce our consumption of CFCs by way of prohibition where alternatives already
Alternatives to Refrigerants
exist, for example, paper products instead of CFC foams for consumer packaging of food and otherwise, or, for instance, by following the lead of the Ontario Government and putting a national tax on motor vehicle air-conditioning to reduce its attractiveness to the consumer, something we did in the mid-1970s.
Of course, the role of industry here is very important. The major producers of CFCs are Dupont, Imperial Chemical Industries and Allied Signal. They must make major commitments to the development of alternative products, and I believe they accept that ozone depleting CFCs must be eliminated from use as soon as possible. There is also a role for the consumer, that is the reduction in our consumption of CFCs by way of prohibition where alternatives already exist, and 1 have already mentioned substituting paper products instead of CFC foams for consumer packaging and putting a national tax on motor vehicle air-conditioning.
The Government could also introduce labelling requirements that identify products containing CFCs so that consumers can make an informed choice.
Inevitably, when we explore an issue of this kind, we have to conclude that there is a necessity to elaborate on the question of climate protection policy. It seems to me that as a first priority, the Government of Canada should launch a global climate protection initiative. This requires long-term thinking, the ability to start in motion programs that will last far beyond the normal political term and which may, indeed, offer little in the way of short-term political gain. But it must be done. We must, as elected representatives, accept this responsibility and challenge if Canada and the world, for that matter, is to be a productive and hospitable place for future generations.
I would like to bring to your attention, Madam Speaker, the fact that West German parliamentarians are already considering how to tackle this very problem. I will list some of the principles they have proposed; first, the examination and understanding of the role of nitrogen dioxide and halogenated hydrocarbons; second, the necessity of assessing the contribution of methane to the greenhouse effect, identifying emission sources and developing international measures to set limits to emissions; third, assessing the disintegration products of halogenated hydrocarbons and their impact on humans and the environment; and fourth, to develop hydrogen fusion energy as a strategy to reverse the global warming trend. In these few words there is a complex and long-term problem. The fifth principle is to urge international co-operation in the maintenance of tropical forests described by scientists as the "lungs of the planet". Finally, the necessity of considering debt-waiving for Third World countries and other measures as a necessary premise for the switch to an environmentally supportable economy. These are items which are being discussed in the Parliament of the Federal Republic of Germany which struck me as being far-reaching and worthwhile to put on record here.

January 21, 1988
Alternatives to Refrigerants
On September 19 the Citizen published an article by Gwynne Dyer. He put the problem this way, and I quote:
There is a serious defect in the human system. We can respond with fear, a sense of urgency and a high degree of co-operation and self sacrifice to present, highly visible emergencies. But we have no built-in sense of alarm when confronted only with a rate of change that augurs disaster for the future.
By the time most people begin to feel the effects personally and develop the sense of urgency that would provide broad political support for drastic corrective action, it will be very late in the process. Perhaps too late, for all these processes will be moving very fast by then, and probably interacting to produce synergistic effects that may be beyond our ability to control.
The article is entitled "Ozone treaty no triumph, but its a first step". Mr. Dyer continues:
That is why the Montreal Protocol is hardly an unqualified triumph. The action it promises is slow and inadequate, and it took 10 years to get even this degree of agreement, although the Global CFC industry only has a gross annual value of about $1 billion. We are still a long way from even such limited international agreements to protect the environment where really rich and powerful interests are involved.
But there is cause for at least a minor celebration. As Mostafa Tolba, executive director the United Nations Environment Programme, said at the signing ceremony: "This is the first truly global treaty that offers protection to every single human being on the planet". True, it doesn't offer much protection, but the precedent is vitally important.
For the first time, sovereign states have formally recognized that their domestic activities affect the environment globally, and that they are accountable for the consequences. Now what we need is about a dozen more treaties of the same kind on various other environmental issues, each having far bigger teeth than this timid firstborn.
That is the end of the article which, I think, expresses very well, in a balanced form, the achievements so far and the challenge still ahead.
To conclude, I would like to read from the book entitled Our Common Future which is the report by the World Commission on Environment and Development, and specifically from the Foreward by Madam Brundtland, the Prime Minister of Norway and the chairperson of that commission, which sat for three years and produced this significant report in April, 1987. Madam Brundtland writes, and I quote:
Scientists bring to our attention urgent but complex problems bearing on our very survival: a warming globe, threats to the Earth's ozone layer, deserts consuming agricultural land. We respond by demanding more details, and by assigning the problems to institutions ill equipped to cope with them. Environmental degradation, first seen as mainly a problem of the rich nations and the side effect of industrial wealth, has become a survival issue for developing nations.
I commend these lines to you, Madam Speaker, which contain a lot of wisdom and the political capacity of putting together in that statement the developed nations of the northern hemisphere with the developing nations of the southern hemisphere and thus creating a common global denominator which is so important in moving ahead with this particular issue.
I want to thank you, Madam Speaker, and my colleagues, who in their wisdom decided to move ahead on this motion we are debating today, urging the Government of Canada to intensify the research for alternatives to refrigerants. It is a small motion but behind its wording is a warning of some significance. In the end, when we examine this issue, we will inevitably have to deal with the question of climate as well as
the welfare and the well-being of future generations of human beings on this planet of ours.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT ADVISABILITY OF INTENSIFYING RESEARCH FOR ALTERNATIVES TO REFRIGERANTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on behalf of the Government and the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan), I am very pleased to have an opportunity to speak on the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia).
When we look at this motion from the outside we see that it speaks to intensifying research, but on the inside it explores the political will that our Government has to protect the atmospheric global commons and the common atmospheric heritage of mankind. There should be no doubt whatsoever in anyone's mind in this House or across Canada with regard to the high priority that the Government places on protecting the ozone layer.
In Montreal on September 16, 1987, an unprecedented international protocol to protect the earth's ozone layer was adopted by over 40 countries. The protocol, developed under the auspices of the United Nations Environmental Program, will slash emission of ozone-depleting emissions of chloro-fluorocarbons, CFCs, by 50 percent. It is the first ever global atmospheric treaty, now known as the Montreal Protocol.
We should be proud of the key role that Canada played in the work which led up to this historic signing. Canada's participation in this issue, both on the national front and on the international plane, merits mention.
Canada is one of the small number of nations which has taken substantial individual action to reduce the use of CFCs, a group of industrial chemicals threatening the ozone layer. In 1980, Canada banned the use of CFCs as a propellant in deodorants, anti-perspirants and hair sprays. Notwithstanding, the threat to the ozone layer remains a global problem requiring a global solution.
Consequently, Canada has played a key role in international negotiations to protect the ozone layer and to develop worldwide controls on ozone-modifying substances. In 1981, Canada strongly supported a proposal that an international treaty be developed to protect the ozone layer. Under the United Nations Environmental Program representatives of some 30 nations have been meeting regularly since 1982 to hammer out the world's first global agreement on the atmospheric environment.
Regionally, opinion was sharply divided among many nations on just how CFCs and other ozone-modifying chemicals were to be restricted. Several times when the talks had broken down completely it was Canadian initiatives that reopened the serious negotiations. The Canadian delegation rapidly gained the reputation not only for the source of its motivation, environmental protection rather than economic self-interest, but also for developing compromise positions and helpful and innovative new ideas to bring together.
January 21, 1988

When it became apparent that an environmentally significant agreement on the control of ozone-modifying chemicals would be difficult to reach, Canada was one among the first nations which supported signing an agreement in principle first and then negotiating the controls later. Thus, in 1985, 28 nations, including Canada, met in Austria to sign the Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer.
The Vienna Convention establishes a framework to protect the earth's atmosphere through co-operative international efforts. It also provides for international co-operation in scientific research and information exchange. Canada signed the agreement in 1985 and was the first nation formally to ratify it in June of 1986. To date, 28 countries have signed the convention. About 10 have ratified it. Canada is hopeful that the required number of ratifications, which is 20, will be attained shortly and that the convention will come into effect this year.
As noted, Canada worked with other nations to develop international pollution control standards to limit the release of ozone-modifying substances. Canada was advocating both a short-term and a long-term strategy, one that would see both the phase-down in production and release of CFCs, and one that would control other ozone-modifying substances as well. These standards were enshrined in the protocol to the Vienna Convention at the diplomatic conference in Montreal on September 14 to 16, 1987.
Throughout the lengthy negotiations to develop both the Vienna Convention and the subsequent pollution control standards, Canada has played a key role. It was a Canadian proposal presented in 1986 which broke a serious deadlock in the negotiations and paved the way for the development of the final pollution control agreement in which Canadian contributions played an important part. In recognition of Canada's efforts, the United Nations Environmental Program accepted Canada's offer to host the diplomatic conference for the signing of this international agreement.
The controls set out in the Montreal Protocol, when implemented, will truly represent a major landmark in history. They will not only represent the first real international action to protect the global atmospheric environment, but also mark the first concerted international effort to prevent an atmospheric environmental problem before it reaches the crisis stage. The Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer and the Montreal Protocol on substances that deplete the ozone layer will become a global turning point, a model for continued world-wide co-operation between Government, industry and public interest groups to safeguard our planet.
I am very proud of the major role which the Government and the Minister of the Environment played in making this happen. Consider for a moment the following. The Montreal Protocol will initiate a dynamic process for responding to all
Alternatives to Refrigerants
ozone layer depleting substances, not just those currently earmarked for control measures. It will provide a mandated phase-down for the most harmful chemicals. This has already stimulated the search for environmentally appropriate substitutes and will ultimately dramatically affect the marketplace. It will provide an incentive for less developed countries to avoid recreating the problem or repeating our mistakes. It will provide stringent trade sanctions against countries which do not join the protocol and refuse to accept their environmental obligations to future generations.
It is the first global treaty to protect the atmosphere from the possible effects of human activity. It is also the first global treaty to mandate controls before significant destruction and economic loss occurs. It demonstrates that Government, industry and other interested parties can set aside parochial interests and work together to preserve the common heritage of mankind.
It demonstrates that global agreements on environmental risk management are possible. It offers a global precedent for controls on toxic chemicals and perhaps even acid rain. For the protocol to come into force it will need to be ratified by a minimum number of countries. Canada will be among the first to do so under the authority of the new Environmental Protection Act currently before the legislative committee. Canadians should be proud of the important role Canada played in the development and signing of this historic agreement.
The Government is committed to achieving the 50 per cent reduction in emissions of controlled CFCs in Canada as set out in the protocol and more. The federal Government is not currently conducting research on alternatives to CFCs. However, we are meeting with the various industrial associations to review their respective programs.
There is a tremendous amount of research going on in the private sector. When all of these consultations are complete, and the ongoing research programs reviewed, then the Government will be in a position to decide whether there is any compelling need to intensify sponsored government research in this area.
I hope that this short intervention demonstrates clearly the responsible actions that our Government is taking and will continue to take to respond to the ozone layer depleting problem.
IMs. Lynn IVlcDonald (Broadview-Greenwood): Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in the debate this afternoon on a very wise and far-reaching proposal put forward by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) which states:

January 21, 1988
Alternatives to Refrigerants
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of intensifying research for alternatives to refrigerants, such as freon, which contain chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) that erode the earth's ozone layer.
It is a very simple proposition, and I am sorry that the response of the Government has not been more forthright.
Yes, Canada has played an important role in the Vienna Convention and the signing of the Montreal Protocol, certainly a global first for a strategy to reduce the emission of substances which deplete the ozone layer. We were very pleased to see that, although I am certainly going to suggest that we ought to be a little cautious as to how fortunate those results might be because it is a very modest first step on a problem on which we still have a great deal more to do.
Canada can be congratulated for its role there. But 1 am sorry that we see so much complacency that that seems to be adequate. The Parliamentary Secretary referred to the consultations with industry and that they will consult and see how much research they are doing. Industry may need a little more of a prod. Perhaps consumers need both a prod and a carrot. We need to see government action in terms of its own purchasing. We as consumers large and small can also play a role in safeguarding our environment. Indeed, on the question of ozone depletion, consumers have been prominent in the struggle. It was consumers who first of all took aerosol cans off the market and required that a substitute product be used. Consumer action can be extremely important in this regard. As a major consumer, Government can also be extremely important. Taxation policies have to be addressed as well as regulations. I am afraid that we have a very long way to go, and complacency that we are getting there is not very helpful.
Let us be clear about what the Montreal Protocol is going to achieve. As the Parliamentary Secretary stated, it was a compromise solution. Canada helped to work out the compromise. Certainly, a compromise to get something signed and something done in order to take that first step was worth taking. It was very important, but let us not think that it is enough. We do not know if it is enough. There is a lot of scientific doubt about it.
Approximately 10 years ago when the scientists themselves began to see the ozone depletion, they did not even publish the results because they were so amazed at the findings. They thought that their instruments were wrong. The problem was so mind-boggling that there could be this major depletion of ozone. Of course, the ozone hole has expanded enormously since then. We do not know if the measures that are being contemplated now will be remotely enough. They are only directed at a reduction, not an elimination. In some countries it is expected that there will be an increase in the use of substances that deplete the ozone layer. Then perhaps there will be a stabilizing and a falling off.
We know that because of the nature of these substances already the massive quantity of those ozone depleting substances are in the air and moving upwards. They have a long lifespan of 75 or 125 years. These chemical reactions of substances thought to be quite inert and harmless, substances that were welcomed by industry and consumers and that
seemed to be an advance, that were non-toxic and not harmful to the health, over time, it turned out, that with chemical reactions in the stratosphere proved to have an extremely harmful effect on human health. They are harmful in terms of skin cancer, they have an effect on food production, and they contribute to the greenhouse effect, with consequences that are so enormous we can scarcely imagine them, climatic warming, raising of ocean levels, and perhaps a complete change in the geography of our country. These are the types of effects that we are talking about.
Yet what does the protocol direct itself to? First a stabilization of the production and emission of these products; then a reduction, not an elimination. We do not know if that reduction will be enough. Perhaps the scientists themselves do not know if it will be enough. Perhaps it was just a situation that that was all that could be achieved politically. Some countries, countries influenced by their own industries that are looking at short-term cost savings and not long-term costs to the environment and human health, stated that that was as far as they were prepared to go.
We have a very major problem yet to solve. We don't know, perhaps the measures are already too late. These processes will continue. Even if we completely stop the emission of these substances into the atmosphere it might be too late, given the quantity that is there already and in the process of these complex chemical reactions.
Practically speaking, what are we looking at? We are looking at substances such as solvents, coolants, substances that go into motor vehicles, air-conditioners, refrigeration, solvents used for electrical equipment, and fast-food packaging. There has been a substitute for aerosol cans. For some of those products there is obviously an alternative immediately available, cardboard for this foamy kind of substance. For other areas, there will have to be more imaginative solutions. It is encouraging to see things like solar run refrigerators, for example. For other substances such as air-conditioners, it is not clear what the substitutes will be, or if the substitutes that are being considered will be quite good enough. More research will be required.
Government policy in terms of taxation can also be very helpful to prod people not to use substances that will have economic, health, and environmental consequences and to use them more sparingly. Of course, one way is to make those unsafe substances more costly to encourage the use of environmentally health conscious benign substances. That is the type of direction in which we have to go.
It is for that reason that I very much welcome the proposal of the Hon. Member for Davenport. It is one that encourages the Government into stimulating research in this area. I would hope that the Government would see fit to support it and not to sit back on its laurels and talk about the good things that have happened. Yes, some good things have happened. Yes, we have made a step. Yes, we have a framework. But let us address this very serious problem with the appropriate kind of response. Let us look at the Brundtland report of the World Commission on the Environment and Development, and the commitment to sustainable development.
January 21, 1988

What could be more fundamental for sustainable development than the survival of this protective layer, the ozone layer around the planet? If we do not have that, then we are talking about very small matters indeed once that is destroyed.
The protection of our planet itself and of human, plant, and animal life on that planet is at risk. It is absolutely fundamental that we give this priority. I share the frustration with the Hon. Member who introduced this motion. It is difficult to talk about matters so important when the impact is such a slow incremental one. Perhaps it is not even that slow. It is fast enough, I guess. It is not like a chemical spill where we see the consequences immediately-one day something is fine and the next day it is contaminated. It has a gradual effect, and it is very much harder to raise the alarm as to the consequences to human health and the environment when the effects are ones which will take place years later.
People are using ordinary consumer products now and years later these elements, having gone through a very complex chemical reaction, will have the effect of depleting the ozone and depriving us of that protective layer, with dire consequences for all life on our planet.
It is a complex matter in which we must involve all people. We must involve consumers and Governments. There must be a research role. I very strongly support the motion and urge the Government to give it the appropriate, very favourable, very enthusiastic, and very serious response it deserves.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT ADVISABILITY OF INTENSIFYING RESEARCH FOR ALTERNATIVES TO REFRIGERANTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to join in the debate on this very important matter. Many people in the country have yet to grasp the importance of the protection of the ozone layer.
I should like to refer to the December issue of Bridges which contained an article referring to the danger or the threat to the ozone layer. The article concluded by indicating on the positive side that a global UNEP treaty had been designed to protect the ozone layer and that the level of knowledge had advanced. It went on to indicate that it has never been more true that the need for scientific research is imperative and exceeded only by the need for international recognition that short-sightedness and narrow self-interest put us all in peril.
I commend the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) for highlighting this subject matter. I say to him and to the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Ms. McDonald) that while the motion suggests that we consider the advisability of intensifying research, the Government of Canada has already actively entered into a program to work toward the coordination of testing, research, and product development of less hazardous product use. As a clear demonstration of this, the Hon. Member for Scarborough Centre (Mrs. Browes) already pointed to the Montreal Protocol. In September, 1987 Canada hosted a gathering of 40 countries in Montreal to negotiate a protective control protocol on the use of CFCs.
Just recently, from January 13 to January 15, 1988, Canada, along with the Conservation Foundation and the
Alternatives to Refrigerants
United States Environmental Protection Agency, co-sponsored in Washington a conference to explore the current scientific status of research and product development of substitutes.
For those who are not familiar with the Conservation Foundation, let me point out that it is a non-profit environmental agency in the United States organized to conduct research on emerging environmental issues, and obviously this matter is one of them. It brings together people with varied backgrounds-academic and scientific-to clarify issues and to reach agreement on what might be done. It communicates the findings of its work to policy makers, parliamentarians like ourselves, and opinion leaders in business, academic circles, the conservation community, and the press. Since its founding in the United States in 1948, the Conservation Foundation has been dedicated to improving the quality of the environment in all respects and to promoting wise use of the earth's resources.
I am happy to report that the conference in Washington was a tremendous success. They had planned for some 250 participants, and over 700 showed up representing industry, environmental groups, and Governments from over 20 countries. Happily there was a clear consensus on the need for action now, and industry described ways and means to introduce new programs designed to reduce emissions and to find environmentally acceptable substitutes for CFCs and halons.
For example, the major producers of these chemicals announced a joint toxicity testing program costing some $8 million to facilitate information transfer and thereby speed up the process of bringing environmentally acceptable substitutes to the market as hastily as possible.
In general terms the conference facilitated the collection and sharing of information on current technologies to reduce emissions of CFCs and halons, including substitute chemicals, recycling, recovery, and destruction. It facilitated the provision of a forum in which users, producers, researchers, regulators, environmental groups, and the media could discuss the development of product substitutes and alternative processes. It facilitated the making of pronouncements by industry that it is or intends to move away from those chemicals and products which are hazardous to the ozone layer. In addition, it facilitated the exchange of information on declining markets for controlled substances and on emerging markets for substitutes and alternatives to CFCs and halons. This is of great advantage to all.
The conference identified ways, means, and opportunities for reducing dependence on CFCs and halons through four separate plenary sessions and a series of workshop sessions. The workshops ran simultaneously with the plenary sessions, and each concentrated on a key application of CFCs and halons. The workshops offered sessions on alternative technologies and substitute products. Each focused on particular chemical substitutes, giving conference participants an opportunity to discuss one or many hazardous products.

January 21, 1988
Alternatives to Refrigerants
In addition, during the two informal "poster paper" sessions, participants had the opportunity to discuss papers and ideas with scientists and engineers working on new developments in the field. The conference featured as well the very practical side effect of a trade fair where commerce could display products and services to all who were interested in the problem. Participants had the opportunity to learn first-hand about the substitutes and alternatives to CFCs and halons which are now being offered.
I have intentionally provided much detail on the successful event just completed in Washington in an effort to underscore the importance which is being placed on the issue not only by the Government but by the private sector, environmental groups, and the public at large. The collective commitment to finding solutions to the ozone layer depletion problem rang clear in Washington with the level of participation and the quality and quantity of information willingly exchanged.
Having looked at the clock, Madam Speaker, let me move on to my concluding paragraph. 1 hope that the comments which have already been made indicate the Government's high priority for this very severe problem. Major efforts are already under way devoted to putting in place substitute chemicals, substitute technologies, and suitable substitute products. Canadians in both the private and public sectors are involved in many of these projects either as participants or in a managerial capacity. Should any priority research area be identified by anyone as requiring additional information or attention, the Government, as is its custom, will give the matter the importance it deserves.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT ADVISABILITY OF INTENSIFYING RESEARCH FOR ALTERNATIVES TO REFRIGERANTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to join in this debate on a very important matter. Before I begin I want to commend the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) for bringing this motion before the House. The Hon. Member has brought many environmental concerns before this House and I commend him for doing so and I want to support this motion.
Research on substitutes to ensure and secure an orderly transition to chemicals and products which will not adversely affect our ozone layer remains a critical element in the timely resolution of this problem. I am happy to be able to report that an unprecedented level of research is now moving forward on several fronts.
Growing concern within the international scientific community, as well as the expectation by industry of regulatory measures to control ozone modifying substances, have revived the quest for alternatives to chlorofluorocarbons or CFCs. Alternatives are being sought in three areas: alternative chemicals; products and services; and technologies.
First, producers of CFCs have concentrated their efforts on alternative chemicals with lower ozone depleting potential. Although many hurdles such as acute toxicity and technical
feasibility have been successfully passed, some technical aspects such as catalyst selection surrounding the development of economically viable commercial processes remain unsolved.
Second, alternative products and services currently exist. For example, fibreglass insulation, though not as efficient per unit volume as polyurethane foam, can be used as a suitable substitute. Another example is egg containers, which do not require foam plastics. As well, aerosol products in many instances are now propelled by hydrocarbons. However, these alternative products and services will require that a price be paid, be it in either efficiency, increased safety or simply consumer preference.
The third alternative is new technology. Alternative technologies currently exist for some products and are under development for others. For example, the deodorant stick has partially replaced the aerosol propellant package. A new helium-based refrigeration system has been developed by Cryodynamics under the sponsorship of NASA in the United States. An aqueous cleaning technology for the electronics manufacturing industry is being substituted for CFC-based cleaning technologies. Last, but by no means least, procedures and work practices could also be re-designed to accommodate recycling of CFCs and minimize emissions to the atmosphere.
I would like to focus attention briefly on a special category of chemicals adversely affecting our ozone layer. They are called halons, chemicals which are very similar to CFCs. However, they contain bromine in addition to or in place of chlorine. These are the chemicals used in fire extinguishers. Current production of these chemicals is relatively small, but because they contain bromine they are three to 11 times more destructive of the ozone layer than CFCs. What is also very worrisome is the rapid rate of growth in the use of halons.
Canada does not currently produce any halons. However, we currently import about 0.5 kilotons of the chemical in bulk, and an undetermined amount in small products. Given the enhanced destructive efficiency of the halons, it is estimated that they contribute about 15 per cent of the Canadian chemical contribution to the destruction of the ozone layer.
Environment Canada officials have been consulting with the Canadian fire protection community on ways and means of dealing with the halon problem. That community agrees with the need for controls to protect our environment and prevent the depletion and/or modification of the ozone layer. However, the halons have a very high economic and security value and there are no known substitutes with the same important fire protection characteristics. The fire protection community has been challenged to meet the fire protection needs of Canadian society, whether it be government, financial, transportation, industrial or defence facilities. In many cases use of halons has been the only acceptable means to achieve required fire protection of critical facilities in a safe and effective manner.
January 21, 1988

Halon fire extinguishants are used to protect life and property from the destructive effects of fire. As such, they have some very desirable qualities. The halons do not cause secondary damage. They are highly effective. They are chemically stable and human tolerance to their exposure has proven to be very high. They are the only known fire extinguishants with these combined benefits and properties. However, their cost is very high compared to other extinguishants such as water, carbon dioxide, or dry chemicals. This fact has limited their use to those applications where cost-benefit concerns have been satisfied.
The fire protection community became aware of the importance of the environmental factors and possible destruction of the ozone layer by halons in the fall of 1986. Immediately a study was conducted by the industry to determine use and emission patterns and how emissions could be reduced or, in some cases, eliminated. Data for the study were provided by fire equipment manufacturers, fire equipment distributors and installers. Limited use levels for Canada were agreed to by consensus.
Let me just list a few of the actions these various groups studying the problem have come up with through consensus prior to any regulatory control. I think it is quite significant. First, they conducted a study to determine use and emission levels. Second, they published major articles in the Fire Journal, their most widely-read publication with a circulation of over 30,000 copies, explaining the problem. Third, they conducted major seminars to advise their community of the concerns and to seek solutions. Fourth, they established and financed the program to be administered by the National Fire Protection Association to co-ordinate and fund research, develop new requirements, and monitor program results. They recently proposed a scheme to charge 3 cents to 5 cents per pound of halon produced to create a research fund to find substitutes. Fifth, they are sponsoring an international meeting to raise the awareness of how halons destroy the ozone layer and to solicit even broader co-operation in the search for solutions. Six, they are looking into the possibility of warning labels for their products. Seven, they are exploring new and additional techniques for halon recapture and recycling.
I submit that this list is a good beginning of voluntary action currently undertaken by the fire protection community. It illustrates the kind of concerted and co-operative action which can be cost-effectively undertaken when government, industry and other interested parties are able to work together.
I look forward to the continuing debate on this subject and the vote to come on this motion because it has been designated as a votable motion. I would like to support the motion.

Madam Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to inform the House that yesterday in Montreal, I met with members of the co-ordinating committee for Canadian solidarity with the Haitian people. The people 1 met asked me to inform the Government, and especially the Minister, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), of their views in the House of Commons.
Basically, one of the demands Haitians living in Canada were making on behalf of the Haitian people who are going through a very difficult time, one of their demands when they were still optimistic about the future, was to have a democratic election, for the first time in many years, and perhaps for the first time in their lives, so they could have a democratically elected government. However, we now know the kind of electoral travesty that led to last Sunday's so-called election. The co-ordinating committee would like to see the Canadian Government immediately and unequivocally condemn this illegal government's National Council for its human rights violations in Haiti and refuse to recognize the "Macoute" election held last Sunday. The committee also asks the Government of Canada to deny any formal or informal recognition to the government formed as a result of that election.
Monday, the Minister said in answer to one of my questions that, considering the extremely low-rate of participation, Canada did not recognize this election. That is one point the co-ordinating committee will appreciate.
Second, the Minister said: We intend to review our relations with Haiti, including development aid. Reviewing our relations with Haiti is basically a matter of recognition. Will the Minister, who said publicly that he did not recognize the election, turn around and recognize the Government that is expected to be formed shortly? That is a question the Minister failed to answer, but it is a fundamental one, and we would certainly appreciate the Government giving us a specific and intelligent answer.

January 21, 1988
Adjournment Debate
If the Government does not recognize the election, it would of course be very difficult to recognize the government formed as a result of that election.
The Minister also said he intended to review his development aid program. If that is indeed the case, I think the Minister will have to consider recommendations made by eight non-governmental observers, sponsored by the International Human Rights Federation, who went to observe the election that was supposed to be held last November in Haiti. They returned to Canada and submitted a report with some very specific recommendations on Canadian aid to Haiti.
First of all, these impartial observers suggested that the Canadian Government immediately stop food aid because it is a disincentive to local food production.
Second, the Government should suspend bilateral aid to Haitian government departments and the institutions that are part of these departments, especially the "institutional reform" and "energy" sectors of the Canadian International Development Agency's Program.
Third, to re-examine publicly all assistance programs to Haiti, in consultation with Canadian non-government organizations operating in Haiti.
Fourth, to act in co-operation with other governments to withdraw any direct assistance to the Haitian government.
Fifth, to maintain and reinforce the projects of nongovernment organizations which benefit the basic groups in the community and strengthen the fabric of the Haitian society in areas such as literacy programs, free radio stations, labour unions, and so on, which can truly help the Haitian people to gain eventually a democratically elected government following a really free election by the Haitian population.
It seems obvious that the Canadian Government is embarrassed. On one hand, it gave in good faith its support to an election. It sent all the proper electoral equipment to Haiti, as well as Canadians to ensure the presence of a local force to guarantee a free election. The fact is that this did not happen. First, General Namphy simply cancelled the election, and second, he took action to ensure that the election would take place while the population could not truly exercise its voting rights democratically. We expect answers from the Government, and I trust that these answers will reflect the proposals of the co-ordinating committee of Canadian solidarity with the Haitian people.

speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Champagne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in his intervention yesterday, the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) drew our attention to three points on which I would now like to comment further.
First, he suggested that the Canadian Government supported for months the military junta of General Namphy. I am certain that the Hon. Member would not wish to put the thorny Haitian issue under the impassioned, abusive and unproductive light too often favoured by certain groups.
In reply to his questions, it would be good to recall that the National Government Council or CNG led by General Namphy, whether we like it or not, represents the constitutionally identified authority to govern the affairs of Haiti until February 7, and thus to ensure the transition to a new government. It was therefore impossible not to have proper relations with the CNG. Until November 29, as I believe that everyone will agree, we provided assistance to organize the election, through the CNG as well as the CEP, while remaining concerned about the growing conflict between the two parties. After November 29, we focussed our action on the CNG using the means at our disposal, short of interfering in the internal affairs of an independent country, to remind the Haitian Government of its constitutional obligations each time it took undesirable action. It was without any illusion that we waited until January 17 to express ourselves as we did to avoid being accused of interfering in the internal affairs of another country at such a critical moment as the holding of an election, whatever the quality of this election. Some view this as improper procrastination. I urge them to give serious consideration to what might have been the democratic value of such a premature intervention, not to mention its real influence on the outcome of events.
Secondly, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has already indicated that we were holding consultations with countries concerned over Haiti. A meeting is being organized with the ambassadors of EEC countries that are interested in gaining a better insight into our position. Generally speaking, our partners are now seeking further consultations on the Haitian question. Still it may be too early to conclude that they are prepared to express similar positions in this respect or consider that pressure through their means of assistance might be the most appropriate way to proceed.
The question of possible concerted action remains relevant and is the subject of consultations. I think I can reassure the Hon. Member by saying that the assistance program is indeed part of the review process with respect to our relations with Haiti. Contrary to a number of blatant allegations, the Government does not fear that our financial assistance might be diverted towards questionable endeavours. However it would rather seek agreement with all the organizations involved and, if need be, make adjustments so that there be no doubt left as to our intentions and actions.
LICENCES IN NOVA SCOTIA/REQUEST FOR CANCELLATION OF LICENCES

Mr. Speaker, on January 19, 1988, I put a question to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Siddon) concerning the irregular issuing of four new Class A lobster licences. 1 asked the Minister to cancel those licences in view of a number of factors that would have to be taken into consideration.
January 21, 1988

By awarding these four new Class A lobster licences, the Minister has broken an undertaking he gave to the Lobster Advisory Committee, which advises him on such matters, and therefore has undermined the integrity of the entire fisheries management system on the East Coast.
Four new Class A licences were given to the offshore fleet when the inshore fleet is struggling to make a living. I might say that this year has been better than most as far as lobster catch is concerned, but the Minister took it upon himself to reverse an undertaking he gave to the Lobster Advisory Committee six months prior to the awarding of these licences. His undertaking was that he would consult with the Lobster Advisory Committee prior to the issuing of new lobster licences. As I indicated to the House, the Minister broke that undertaking.
When one considers the recipients of these new four Class A licences, one must call into serious question the patronage which is being exhibited by the Government of Canada. It is a well known fact that the individuals involved were known supporters and affiliates of the Conservative Party of Canada. That does not mean one ought not to be given an opportunity to make an application for various licences because one holds a particular political belief, but, on the other hand, it is very clear and obvious to many that the system we have in Atlantic Canada for issuing lobster licences was circumvented in this particular instance and four prominent supporters of the Conservative Party were able to obtain those licences and the largesse that goes along with those new four Class A lobster licences.
In fact, in August last year, the Minister took it upon himself to meet with two companies that I am aware of, and perhaps with even more privately, at the Prince George Hotel in Halifax. These two companies were Comeau Seafoods and Newell Lobsters. A business partner of Newell Lobsters just happens to be a Conservative MLA in Nova Scotia.
I am not suggesting any impropriety by the sitting MLA in Nova Scotia, but I am suggesting very clearly that there is a perception, and I believe it to be a real perception, that the only reason the recipients of those licences in Nova Scotia were successful in getting them is because of their affiliation and contacts with the Conservative Party of Canada. That is shameful, in view of the fact there is a large inshore fishery in Nova Scotia and the Atlantic region whose economic interests the Minister has sacrificed in order to soothe and facilitate his political friends who are operating boats on the offshore.
I think it rather repugnant that the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans would stand in the House and refuse to cancel those licences. It is so repugnant that the Premier of the Province of Nova Scotia has called for cancellation of those licences. The Minister of Fisheries in Nova Scotia has called for the cancellation of those licences. The Leader of the Liberal Opposition in Nova Scotia, who brought this issue to the forefront, has also called for the cancellation, as have
Adjournment Debate
fishing groups, unions, and so on, in the Atlantic region. Yet this Government continues to wear the label of sleaze and patronage. When it has an opportunity, it refuses to seize the opportunity to cancel those licences and thereby restore confidence and integrity to the management system in the fisheries in Atlantic Canada. By supporting the inshore fishermen as opposed to the offshore fishermen, it would certainly rid itself of the label and symbolism of patronage, sleaze, and so on.
I hope the response from the Parliamentary Secretary today will provide us with new information, that it will now cancel those licences, since it has circumvented the process which has been put in place for many years. If he would do that, I am sure all those individuals, including myself, who have spoken out fairly forcefully on this issue, would compliment the Minister for taking this action. He now knows that the action he did take by issuing those licences was certainly not in the best interest of the inshore fishermen or, indeed, the Atlantic fisheries as a whole.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the selection procedures for issuing new offshore lobster licences are similar to those used for new licences in other fisheries. The Department provided the Minister with a list of 13 applicants and a list of criteria which ideally could be met by candidates and against which they could be evaluated. Based on an evaluation, he chose the four applicants which best fit the criteria. The strongest candidate met all the criteria and received two licences. The other two were stronger than the remaining candidates and each received one licence.
In discussions over the past two years, lobster fishermen have stressed that no new inshore or offshore licences should be issued in traditional South West Nova fishing zones. They argue that no new fishing effort could be accommodated on these zones 4X and 5. The Minister has heeded this advice. There have been no new inshore licences in these traditional zones. What has happened is the Minister, based on advice from officials, has opened a new fishing zone in area 4W eastern Nova Scotia and allowed four new licences to harvest a developmental quota of 360 tonnes in that area.
In order to lessen the risk for the new participants in this fishery, he has allowed each of the new licences to have 30 tonnes, 120 tonnes in total, in the traditional offshore area 4X and 5 and reduced the over-all enterprise allocations of the original eight licences by a corresponding amount of 120 tonnes. To compensate the original licence holders, they have been given 15 tonnes each in the new zone. Let me repeat, the total offshore quota in 4X and 5 remains at 720 tonnes. It has not increased. In summary, the Minister has not increased effort in the 4X and 5 area and this was consistent with the advice of the committees.

Madam Speaker, on January 18, I put several questions to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret) with respect to the awarding by the Government of the CF-18 contract to Canadair in Montreal rather than to Bristol Air in Winnipeg. That is a decision which has infuriated people from all sectors of the communities in Manitoba.
I asked the Minister why he had told the Leader of the New Democratic Party, who asked about this decision and who asked for assurances that the decision was made on the basis of an analysis of the competitive bids, and the Minister said that the Government had done that. The Leader of the New Democratic Party also asked why the Minister did not agree to the proposal that the New Democratic Party made, that the decision be looked into by the Auditor General. This is a proposal that was rejected by the Minister.
We now know, as a result of information obtained by The Globe and Mail and the Winnipeg Free Press, that the decision was made for political reasons. The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion said in the House that the two bids were very close on technical merit and on cost, and that the results were very close between two highly competent groups of companies. Outside the House he said that the Canadair bid was $104 million over three and a half years compared with $105 million for Bristol.
We now know that according to the evaluation done for the Department by its technical experts that the facts are incorrect. In fact, what the experts said was that the Canadair bid would cost 13 per cent more in the first four years. With regard to the question of technical merit, they said that while both companies were technically acceptable, Bristol was the preferred bid based on "a significantly higher technical assessment". The people of Manitoba have every reason to continue to be angry with the Government for its wrongful decision.
The second question 1 asked the Minister was in connection with the report in the Winnipeg Free Press that highly-placed senior public servants had made it very clear that in the decision as to which universities would be chosen to receive funding as centres of scientific excellence that Manitoba universities would be frozen out because of the fact that the Premier of Manitoba, Mr. Pawley, has opposed so many of the recommendations of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), such as the free trade agreement. The fact is that the Prime Minister's proposal that the Government of Canada allocate $1.3 billion of new money for improving the quality of our higher education system and the establishment of the centres
of excellence at a number of universities in Canada to concentrate on scientific research and development does not deal with new money at all.
The fact is that the Prime Minister, before he became the Prime Minister, criticized former Liberal Governments for their failures to adequately fund scientific research and development. He pointed out quite correctly that in Canada we were spending about 1.5 per cent of Gross National Product on research and development and that this was among the lowest of any of the countries belonging to the OECD, as well as Japan. He promised that a Conservative Government would increase expenditures to 2.5 per cent of Gross National Product.
We know now that in fact expenditures are still at the level they were during the Liberal years, that is 1.3 per cent. We know now that business and industry have not responded as the Conservatives promised they would to increase significantly their expenditures and their efforts in the field of scientific research and development. We know now that Canada is near the bottom, if not right at the bottom, of all the countries in the western world, including Japan, in terms of the efforts that are made in the field of scientific research and development. We know now that after the Conservative Government took office it realized what a tremendous scam and scandal had been created by the Liberal Government scientific research credit fund, which was supposed to encourage industry to participate in and increase its efforts in scientific research, and that it would probably cost the treasury of Canada and the people of Canada approximately $800 million. In fact, it would cost a great deal more.
The Conservatives announced the stoppage of that plan, but they grandfathered all those already in the pipeline. The result is that Canadian taxpayers will probably lose approximately $3 billion. In fact, very little in the way of real research has been done.
I say that it is time for the Government to face up to realities. It is time to stop playing politics when handing out contracts. It is time to live up to the promise made by the Prime Minister when he was the Leader of the Opposition, that the Conservative Government would substantially increase the efforts of Canada in the field of scientific research and development.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I listened with considerable interest to my NDP friend telling us about the CF-18 maintenance contracts, but I found rather strange his reluctance to provide all the figures. Although he and the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) may not know it, the CF-18 maintenance contract was in two parts. The first part dealt with engineering and the second with repairs.
January 21, 1988

In his remarks, the Hon. Member said that, compared with Canadair, Bristol's bid was 13 per cent lower on the engineering side. What he failed to indicate, however, is that Canadair's bid on the repairs side was 10.5 per cent lower than Bristol's.
Well, Madam Speaker, if we consider the situation and the contract as a whole, we realize, as the Treasury Board minister indicated at the time, that there was some 3 per cent differential on the basis of which the Conservative government, anxious to promote national and collective interests-a notion which may escape the NDP member, let alone his leader- ruled in favour of Canadair.
It is on the basis of its concern for national identity and the equitable sharing of contracts that the federal government following various departmental assessments on technical merits and costs decided, under the circumstances, to award the contract to Canadair.
Adjournment Debate
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, may I tell my honourable friend that we have provided the Auditor General with the documents he was seeking and that the government would gladly and at any time provide ... Of course, there remains the condition of confidentiality for the bids made by existing companies, but whenever the Auditor General wants to have a look at bid papers, Madam Speaker, the minister will gladly provide them, as tradition will have it. Again, the Progressive Conservative Government is demonstrating that it is accountable for its decisions which are based on the need to promote national unity and equitable sharing of contracts among all Canadians.
